▪ Chronic: HF, VT/VF, systemic embolization, may be asymptomatic




▪ ECG w/ persistent STE




▪ TTE, other imaging (CMR, CT, ventriculography)




▪ Acute: CHF rx, ACEi, avoid NSAIDs/steroids, start heparin (if EF<35%)




▪ Chronic: ACEi, , diuretics, AC (if EF<35%)




▪ Surgical repair




LV Thrombus




▪ 5% of AMI patients post- PCI (usually LV apex)




▪ Large infarct size, severe apical akinesis or dyskinesis, LV aneurysm, anterior MI




▪ Can form 24-72h post MI




▪ 90% of thrombi at 2w




▪ Embolization risk persists for 6mo but most by 3-4mo; risk 10% if not on AC




▪ TTE w contrast




▪ CMR or CT




▪ Warfarin (INR 2-3); DOAC may be alternative (Circ. 2022;146:e205–e223)




▪ When to stop AC unclear, check for thrombus on TTE at 3-6mo




Pericarditis




▪ Peri-MI pericarditis has decreased with PCI




▪ Friction rub within 2-3 days post MI. Often large infarct




▪ 10% at 2-4d post-transmural MI




▪ May be focal or diffuse




Dressler’s syndrome (1-6wks): malaise, fever, leukocytosis, late autoimmune carditis, rare




▪ ECG (diffuse STE, PR depressions)




▪ TTE (effusion)




▪ CMR or cardiac CT




▪ ASA + colchicine




▪ Avoid NSAIDs and steroids post MI




▪ See Pericarditis





URGENT ASSESSMENT OF POST-MI COMPLICATION
• PAGE Cardiology (STAT)




• Assess for instability, focused physical exam (new murmur, pericardial friction rub, elevated JVP, crackles, access site(s))




• STAT labs (troponin, PT/INR, VBG, PTT, T&S, BMP, CBC, LFT, lactate), ensure adequate vascular access (≥2 PIVs)




• Run telemetry, repeat ECG, STAT TTE, consider STAT CTA if concern for RP bleed/aortic dissection, notify interventional team




ELECTRICAL COMPLICATIONS
Overview




• Bradyarrhythmia/conduction block: may be due to coronary artery occlusion (see below) or baroreceptor reflexes (Anes2003;98:1250)




• Tachyarrhythmia: related to creation of re-entrant circuit from scar formation and/or ↑automaticity from adrenergic surge








Arrhythmia




Location/Mechanism




Incidence/Timing




Treatment/Outcome




aimhtyhrraydarB




Sinus bradycardia




▪ Inferior and posterior MI




▪ Beneficial: ↓myocardial O2 demand




▪ Up to 40% of acute MI




▪ Occurs early in STEMI




▪ Atropine, temp pacing or dopa/epi if unstable




First degree AV block




▪ Inferior: ↑vagal tone or AV node ischemia (RCA), narrow QRS




▪ Anterior: septal necrosis below AV node, RBBB, wide QRS




▪ More common in inferior MI




▪ If due to inferior MI, transient (vagal)




▪ Continue CCB or BB unless PR interval >240ms




Second degree




AV block: Mobitz Type I




▪ Usually inferoposterior MI (↑vagal tone, narrow QRS) or AV node ischemia




▪ Usually within first 24h of MI




▪ Usually transient; observe




▪ Atropine if symptoms or HR <45




Second degree




AV block: Mobitz Type II




▪ Usually anterior MI with infranodal conduction injury, wide QRS, HR often <30bpm, 33% progress to CHB




▪ Usually within first 24h of MI




▪ Consider temporary pacing




▪ In infranodal block, atropine may paradoxically worsen AV block




Third degree AV block (CHB)




▪ If inferior MI: intra-nodal lesion; narrower QRS escape




▪ If anterior MI: infra-nodal lesion; wide, unstable escape rhythm




▪ 3-7% acute MI




▪ Inferior: gradual, stable




▪ Anterior: sudden, 12-24h after MI




▪ Recovery 5-7d; temp pacing required +/- PPM




▪ Inferior: transient, resolves on its own




▪ Anterior: high mortality (80%) and indicates extensive conduction system necrosis




Intraventricular




Conduction Blocks




▪ 50% already present on first ECG, may represent antecedent disease of conduction syndrome




▪ Suggests more extensive infarct




▪ 2-5% of MI




▪ Patients w/ BBB are more likely to have comorbid conditions, larger area infarcts, and higher mortality




ralucirtnevarpuS saimhtyhrrA




Sinus tachycardia




▪ May be compensatory for LV dysfunction, common in anterior MI




▪ Pain, anxiety, pericarditis, fever




▪ 25% of acute MI




▪ Undesirable as ↑myocardial oxygen demand, ↓diastole time causes ↓coronary perfusion




▪ Treat underlying cause




Atrial fibrillation, Atrial flutter




▪ Early: may be transient due to ↑sympathetic; atrial ischemia




▪ Late: due to atrial stretch/HF




▪ 6-8%, may be >30% of acute MI




▪ A/w mortality, particularly if late (>30d) AF (Circ 2011;123:2094)




▪ If unstable, cardioversion; consider BB, amiodarone, digoxin, anticoagulation




saimhtyhrrayhcaT




ralucirtneV




Premature Ventricular Contraction




▪ Due to electrical instability and increased sympathetic tone




▪ Variable




▪ Correct electrolyte deficits, BB. Do NOT treat with anti-arrhythmics as can ↑mortality (NEJM 1991;324:781)




Accelerated Idioventricular Rhythm (AIVR)




▪ 50-110bpm, higher V- vs A-rate; in 40%, considered a reperfusion rhythm




▪ Up to 20% of STEMI




▪ Usually within 12-48h, can occur after reperfusion




▪ Do not treat unless symptomatic or hemodynamically unstable, usually short duration & does not affect prognosis




Ventricular Tachycardia




▪ Monomorphic VT <170bpm is unusual early after STEMI, suggests pre-existing arrhythmogenic scar; recurrent ischemia usually polymorphic VT




▪ NSVT 1-7%, sustained VT (2-3% of STEMI, <1% NSTEMI)




▪ Usually 48h post STEMI, late VT (>48h) has very poor prognosis




▪ Antiarrhythmic agents (amiodarone, lidocaine)




▪ Urgent revascularization if due to ischemia




▪ Cardioversion/defibrillation to prevent VF and restore hemodynamic stability




▪ Correct underlying abnormalities (pH, K, Mg, hypoxemia)




Ventricular Fibrillation




▪ Risk factors: ↑age, prior MI (scar), anterior MI, cardiogenic shock, ↓LVEF, CKD




▪ VF >48h post-MI may indicate LV dysfunction




▪ 5% of STEMI




▪ 1% of NSTEMI




▪ ACLS/defibrillation




▪ Anti-arrhythmic infusion (24-48h amiodarone post-defibrillation)




▪ Maintain K>4, Mg>2.2

topics.title: Cardiac Catheterization
topics.text:
Source content














• Note: RAO caudal: best overall view & best for LCx; LAO caudal: LM, prox LAD, prox LCx; LAO + RAO cran: mid+distal LAD




LEFT VS RIGHT HEART CATHETERIZATION
• LHC: Arterial access (radial, fem). Assess coronary anatomy/lesions (described as coronary angiogram), LV & Ao pressures; PCI




• RHC: Venous access (IJ, fem). Assess hemodynamics (see Pulmonary Artery Catherization); cardiac biopsies (usually RV)




CORONARY ANATOMY
• LCA and RCA & their branches create two rings around the heart: RCA + LCX in AV groove; LAD + PDA in IV groove




• 80% of PDA arises from RCA (right dominant), thus inferior MI more likely due to RCA lesion; 10% from LCx; 10% co-dominant




PREPARATION FOR CATHETERIZATION
• NPO MN vs clear liquid diet at midnight, then NPO 2hr prior (EHJ 2024:45:47) ; INR<2 for radial, <1.8 for fem/IJ; monitor Cr, no ppx abx. Cont ASA, statin, BB. Hold AC (ellucid): UFH gtt (hold when on call), LMWH (hold tx dose 24h prior, DVT ppx 12h prior), DOACs >48hr or >72hr if CrCl<30. Hold metformin (1d pre, 2d post), may hold ACEi or SGLT2i (procedure dependent)




• Document b/l radial, femoral, popliteal, DP pulses, & Allen’s test. Check for bruits. Note history of HIT, PAD, Ao aneurysm/dissection




• Contrast allergy: pre-tx w/ steroids & benadryl if patient has documented allergy.




• Respiratory distress: patient will need to lie flat; consider intubation if prohibitive hypoxemia/pulmonary edema




• Pre-hydration w/ crystalloids and NAC/bicarb have not been shown to prevent CIN in most patients with moderate CKD (Lancet 2017;389:1312; NEJM2018;378:603); CINriskcalculator




PERCUTANEOUS CORONARY INTERVENTION CONSIDERATIONS
• Access: fewer bleeding/vascular complications if radial (vs femoral) esp for PCI iso ACS, possible ↓death in ACS (JACC2018;71:1167); due to radial vasospasm, CCB and/or nitrogylcerin is administered along with UFH to prevent arterial occlusion




• Identifying HD significant lesions: fractional flow reserve (FFR), diastolic hyperemia-free ratio (DFR), and instant wave free ratio (iFR) assess functional impact of lesion; intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) evaluates lumen diameter, lesion length, and lesion calcification




• Contraindications to stents: predicted DAPT non-adherence, anticipated major surgery within treatment time, elevated bleeding risk




• Antiplatelet: 81mg ASA indefinitely (Circ2016;134:e123). P2Y12 inhibitor post cath. DAPT duration decided with interventional team




◦ Not high bleeding risk: ACS → 12mo DAPT; stable IHD → ≥6mo DAPT if DES or ≥1mo if BMS




◦ High bleeding risk: ACS → 6mo DAPT, consider DAPT 1-3mo followed by P2Y12i; stable IHD → ≥3mo DAPT if DES or ≥1mo if BMS, consider 1-3mo DAPT followed by P2Y12i (JACC Cardiovasc Interv 2024;17:2197)




◦ Triple therapy for patients requiring AC: see ACS. Usually, 1 wk triple therapy then P2Y12 inhibitor + DOAC




POST-PROCEDURE CARE
• Femoral access: 4-6h bedrest (HOB<30°) after procedure. Closure devices decrease time needed for bedrest




◦ Groin checks immediately, 6h, 8h post-procedure: check b/l pulses, palpate for pulsatile masses, auscultate for bruits




◦ Sheaths: usually removed when PTT<60, confirm with interventional fellow; only fellows remove sheaths




• Radial access: TR band for 4-6h driven by RN protocol. If paresthesias/numbness, examine, check finger sat probe for perfusion, can remove several mLs of air from band if necessary and if no complications. NOTE: if hematoma do not remove until fellow assesses




POST-CATHERIZATION COMPLICATIONS
• Access site complications: always inform the interventional fellow who performed the procedure, diagnose by exam and US




◦ Hematoma: mass w/o bruit. Apply compression. Fellow may recommend FemoStop device if unable to control




◦ Pseudoaneurysm: pulsatile mass with bruit at access site. Tx w/ compression; if <2cm, may require thrombin injection or surgery if >2 cm. Urgent arterial US & Vascular Surgery consult




◦ AV fistula: continuous bruit with no mass. Evaluate w/ arterial US. Surgical repair usually necessary




◦ Limb ischemia: from thrombus, dissection, or malpositioned closure device. Evaluate pulses, limb warmth, & PVR




◦ Retroperitoneal bleed: presents within hours post-cath, often with hemodynamic instability ± flank pain ± ecchymoses. STAT CT A/P if stable. Obtain large bore IV access, IVF, transfuse, discuss with attending about stopping/reversing anticoagulation




• Other complications:




◦ Infection: higher risk with vascular closure devices




◦ Atheroembolism: eosinophilia; livedo reticularis; blue toes; mesenteric ischemia; acute, subacute, or chronic renal dysfunction




◦ CIN: occurs within 24-72h with peak Cr 1-5d post contrast load; risk correlated with contrast load and initial GFR




◦ Tamponade: narrow PP, hypotension 2/2 coronary/cardiac perf. Check pulsus (>10 mmHg), STAT TTE, alert cath fellow.




◦ MI/CVA: due to in-stent thrombosis (MI) or distal embolization post-cath (CVA). Discuss all CP/neuro changes with cath fellow




◦ Radiation injury: more common in CTO cases; occurs days to weeks after PCI; ranges from erythema to skin ulceration




◦ Delayed Hemostasis: apply indirect pressure several cm cranial to site of skin access. Page gen cards fellow to discuss escalation to cath fellow/vasc surg (see ellucid escalation pathway)

topics.title: Non-Invasive Cardiac Testing

panels.title: ROLE OF NON-INVASIVE CARDIAC TESTING IN CHEST PAIN EVALUATION
Approach to choosing a stressor and evaluation modality:

topics.text:
BASICS
• Non-invasive cardiac testing includes functional and anatomic testing




• Approach to testing: 1) clinical question being asked, 2) symptom acuity, 3) baseline CVD risk/known CAD hx, 4) patient-specific C.I.




• For guideline-based assistance in decision making, use Stressing Wisely. For examples of (+) and (-) tests, use Radiopaedia.




ROLE OF NON-INVASIVE CARDIAC TESTING IN CHEST PAIN EVALUATION





Source: 2021 ACC/AHA Guidelines for Evaluation and Diagnosis of Chest Pain (Circ 2021;144:e368-e454)




Deciding between CCTA (anatomic) and stress imaging in an intermediate-high risk patient:




• CCTA favored: Age<65y and no prior CAD, rule out obstructive CAD, detect non-obstructive CAD, prior functional study w/o conclusive results, bypass graft assessment, known anomalous coronaries, parallel evaluation of aorta, pulmonary arteries, or LAA




• Stress imaging favored: Age>65y, if known >50% (obstructive) CAD to assess for specific areas of ischemia, prior CCTA w/o conclusive results, parallel evaluation for scar or microvascular dysfunction (PET or CMR)




• CCTA has higher sensitivity and similar angiography rates as conventional stress imaging; however, CCTA may lead to better outcomes overall as it can detect non-obstructive CAD and therefore drive preventive care (NEJM 2018;379:924)




STRESS/FUNCTIONAL TESTING
• Indications:




◦ Diagnose CAD: Workup stable angina in pts with intermediate-high risk of CAD. Consider spectrum of non-invasive tests vs. cath in intermediate-risk pts presenting with more acute sx. Not indicated in pts with no symptoms or at low risk




◦ Evaluate new or changing sx concerning for ischemia in pts with known CAD




◦ Post-revascularization: Evaluate pts with angina or asymptomatic pts if incomplete revasc or >2y post-PCI/5y post-CABG.




◦ Pre-op risk assessment: If indicated (see Perioperative Medicine)




◦ Other: Newly diagnosed HF or cardiomyopathy likely secondary to ischemia, functional capacity (for exercise prescription), viability testing, valvular disorders, dobutamine stress echo in LFLG AS, quantify microvascular disease (PET)




• Contraindications: Untreated ACS, MI within 2d, high risk or LM CAD, uncontrolled arrhythmia, ADHF, severe AS or HOCM, recent DVT/PE, acute myo-/peri-/endocarditis, aortic dissection, uncontrolled HTN




• Preparation: NPO 3h prior, longer if imaging or adenosine. Must reverse DNR/DNI for test




◦ If the question is “Does the patient have CAD?” → hold BB and nitrates




◦ If the question is “How well are meds working in known CAD?” → continue BB and nitrates




◦ Hold BB >24h for dobutamine stress test; hold caffeine >12h for adenosine




▪ Positive test results: Optimize medical rx. Decision re: angiography/revascularization varies by pt (degree of sx, tolerance of medical therapy). In ISCHEMIA trial, initial revasc vs. medical therapy did not reduce risk of ischemic CV events for pts with moderate to severe stable ischemic heart disease (NEJM2020;382:1395). In pts w/ stable angina, PCI does not increase exercise tolerance (Lancet 2018;391:31), but for pts who cannot tolerate medical therapy, PCI improved symptoms (NEJM 2023;389:2319)




• Caveats:




◦ Majority of vulnerable plaques are angiographically insignificant (<70% stenosis) → CCTA more sensitive for their detection




◦ Angiographically significant 3VD may produce false-negative vasodilator stress test → ”balanced ischemia”




▪ Balanced ischemia can be detected as transient ischemic dilatation (enlargement of LV cavity during stress)




▪ PET has higher accuracy in 3VD than SPECT/MIBI, because PET quantifies blood flow




.




Approach to choosing a stressor and evaluation modality:
Approach to choosing a stressor and evaluation modality:




• See Table 5 for full list of contraindications by test type (Circ 2021;144:e368-e454).




Choosing a stressor:




◦ Exercise: Preferred if patient can reach goal exertion. More relevant to real-world stress




◦ Adenosine/Regadenoson:




▪ Mechanism: Vasodilation via cAMP, detect ischemia by coronary steal (stenosed coronary arteries are unable to further dilate, creating a relative perfusion deficit in diseased vessels).




▪ Side effects: Wheezing, bradycardia, HoTN. Caution if ACTIVE bronchospasm, high grade AVB, SSS, severe AS




◦ Regadenoson (vs adenosine) has decreased respiratory/conduction side effects, is more cost-effective in obese pts, but caution if seizure hx (reversal agent aminophylline ↑seizure risk)




◦ Dobutamine:




▪ Mechanism: Positive inotropy and chronotropy via β-1 receptor agonism. Extremely high dose (up to 40 mcg/kg/min)




▪ Side effects: tachyarrhyth. Caution if MI <48h, hx malignant arrhyth, sev AS, HOCM, sev HTN, sev PAH, aortic dissection




Choosing an evaluation modality:




◦ ECG: Only used as stand-alone with exercise. Do not use with any longstanding ST/T wave abnormalities.




◦ TTE: Can define ischemia severity and risk-stratify. Additional info on hemodynamics/valves. ECG also obtained simultaneously.




▪ Do not use in pts with LBBB, V-pacing, or extensive wall motion abnormalities at rest




◦ Nuclear imaging (PET or SPECT/MIBI myocardial perfusion imaging):




▪ Uses a radiotracer (MIBI in SPECT, multiple options in PET) to detect areas of ↓perfusion between rest and stress states. Can measure LV function, transient LV dilatation, myocardial blood flow reserve. PET can detect microvascular ischemia.




▪ More expensive than TTE & high amount of radiation (SPECT > PET)




▪ PET more Sn & Sp than SPECT with faster image acquisition. Less widely available & more expensive. Additional uses for imaging in rheumatologic (i.e. cardiac sarcoid) and oncologic contexts (i.e. cardiac myxoma, metastases).




◦ Cardiac MRI (CMR):




▪ Localize ischemia and infarction, assess LV and RV function, determine myocardial viability. Can also detect microvascular dysfunction and tissue properties of the heart (inflammation, scarring, infiltration, cardiac tumors, pericardial disease)




Exercise Tolerance Test (ETT):




• Approach: ETT refers to exercise + ECG (cheap, available), or exercise + imaging eval (TTE, SPECT) (↑sensitivity)




• Protocols: Bruce (large changes in workload between stages), modified Bruce (for less fit pts → adds stages of lower workload)




• Assess: exercise duration, METs, BP/HR response, HR recovery, double product (HR x SBP), DukeTreadmillScore (estimates risk of CAD in pts w/ chest pain undergoing exercise stress testing (Circ1998;98:1622)).




• Diagnostic if: >85% max-predict HR (220-age), peak double product (HRxBP) >20k, HR recovery (HRpeak – HR1min post-exercise) >12, STEs - also localize to vascular territory




• Increased probability of ischemia with: ↑ # of leads with STD especially horizontal or downsloping, ↑ degree of max STD, ↓ METs when ECG changes occur, ventricular ectopy during recovery, increased time to recovery of ECG, failure of SBP to rise with exercise.




Viability testing:




• Indication: Determine viability of ischemic myocardium (assess for hibernating tissue) that may be salvaged w/ revascularization.




• Modalities: SPECT, PET, TTE, MRI with exercise or pharmacologic stress. Looking for metabolic or contractile reserve.




ANATOMIC TESTING
Coronary CTA (CCTA):




• Indications:




◦ Evaluate for the presence and extent of CAD. Primarily anatomic info, though offers plaque characterization and CT FFR.




◦ Asymptomatic pts: NOT for screening use. Low-risk pts with sx: high NPV (99%) for CAD rule-out (JACC2008;52:1724). Moderate-




risk pts with sx: reasonable for risk stratification (especially after equivocal stress test).




• Preparation: Requires cardiac gating (goal HR 60-70, may need to give BB) and respiratory gating (breath hold for 5+ sec).




• Results:




◦ 2y ACS risk significantly elevated if high-risk plaque (16%) and/or stenotic disease (6%) (JACC2015;28:337)




◦ Higher Sn & Sp for coronary stenosis compared to cMRI (Annals2010;152:167)




• Caveats: Less useful in pts with extensive calcifications (older) or stented vessels due to “blooming” artifact (cannot eval patency).




Coronary Artery Calcium (CAC) Scan:




• Indications:




◦ Risk-assessment for ASCVD risk stratification. Used to guide decision-making for primary prevention/statin therapy in asymptomatic pts, ≥40y at intermediate-risk (7.5-19.9% 10y ASCVD risk). DO NOT use in symptomatic pts or high risk pts.




• Preparation: Non-gated, non-contrast (if done independent of CCTA) CT scan.




• Results: MESA score accounts for CAC score and is able to refine 10 year risk estimates




◦ If CAC score 0 and pt without significant risk factors, reasonable to defer statin therapy for up to 5 years (Circ2019;140:496).




◦ If CAC score ≥100 or >75%ile for age & gender, recommend aggressive lifestyle changes, ASCVD RF modification (BP, smoking cessation, diabetes treatment), & statin therapy (JACC2019;73:285)




Cardiac MRI: provides both stress/functional and anatomic testing options

CLINICAL QUESTIONS AND ASSOCIATED TTE FINDINGS

runs.t: CLINICAL QUESTIONS AND ASSOCIATED TTE FINDINGS

topics.text:
Source content



View




Position




View*




PARASTERNAL LONG AXIS




• LV size, function, wall thickness (septum/posterior wall)




• MV/AoV function/flow (w/ Doppler)




• LVOT diameter, aortic root size




• Pericardial effusion




Patient: lying on left side, with left arm under head




Probe: 2-3 inches left of sternum at 3rd-4th intercostal space, indicator at 10 o’clock (facing R shoulder). Should see LA, LV, Ao, RV, and dAorta














PARASTERNAL SHORT AXIS




• Cross-sectional views of the heart from base to apex, at level of AoV, MV and mid- ventricle/papillary muscles




• MV/AoV/RVOT flow (w/ Doppler)




Patient: same as above




Probe: from long axis view, rotate probe clockwise until indicator at 2 o’clock (facing L shoulder). Fan probe to L hip until at level of papillary muscles.














APICAL 4 CHAMBER




• RV/LV size, function, thrombus




• TV/MV function/flow (w/ Doppler)




• Septal size/motion




• Pericardial effusion




• In 5-chamber view, can see AoV and proximal ascending aorta




Patient: lying flat on back or left decubitus




Probe: at PMI w/ probe indicator at 3 o’clock (to the pt’s L). For 5-chamber view, fan probe cranially.














SUBXIPHOID (aka subcostal)




• RV/LV size, function




• Pericardial effusion




Patient: laying flat on back, can slightly bend legs




Probe: below xyphoid process, indicator to pt’s R














INFERIOR VENA CAVA




• IVC diameter and respiratory variation gives estimate of volume status and RA pressure




• Most helpful for extremes of volume (i.e. very dry or very wet)




• Hepatic vein flow reversal




*Images from: Soni, N. J., Arntfield, R., & Kory, P.




(2020). Point of care ultrasound. Elsevier.




Patient: same as above




Probe: rotate 90°, indicator to head. Fan L, rock up















REVIEWING THE MGH REPORT: for questions or clarification of findings, call Echo Lab (x6-8871) or page on-call Echo Fellow
R E V IE W I N G T H E MG H R E P O R T : for questions or clarification of findings, call Echo Lab (x6-8871) or page on-call Echo Fellow




• Valvulopathy: stenosis/regurgitation (valve area, gradients, severity), leaflets, vegetations




Indications for STAT TTE:




• Structure/chamber dimensions: aorta, LVIDd & LVIDs (LV internal diameter in diastole, range: 42 – - Eval hemodynamic instability of




58mm & systole, range: 25 – 40mm), IVS (septum, 6-10mm), PWT (posterior wall thickness, 6-10mm, ↑ suspected cardiac etiology (e.g. post




in LVH, diastolic dysfunction), LV volume (ULN: 74ml/m2 in men 61 inwomen, <40 suggest restrictive), cath / TAVR / PPM placement)




LA volume (ULN: 34ml/m2, ↑in MR/MS, diastolic dysfunction, AF) - Eval for early MI complication




• EF: “preserved” EF ≥50%, “mildly reduced” EF 40-50%, “reduced” EF <40% - Suspected MI w/ non-diagnostic




• WMA: territory correlates w/ coronary vessels (anterior + septal = LAD, inferior = RCA, lateral = LCx). If biomarkers and EKG global WMA, r/o diffuse ischemia vs non-ischemic insult (sepsis, stress) - Identify cause of cardiac arrest




• RVSP: RVSP=4v2 + RAP. RAP assumed to be 10 mmHg and v = TR jet velocity. RVSP >35mmHg (<60yrs) and >40mmHg (> 60yrs) is elevated.




• Shunt detection: agitated saline contrast study (i.e. TTE w/ bubble) to detect PFOs, ASDs, and pulmonary arte-riovenous shunts




CLINICAL QUESTIONS AND ASSOCIATED TTE FINDINGS
C L I N I C A L Q U E S T I O N S A N D A S S O C I A T E D TTE F I N D I N G S




• Right heart strain in acute PE: RV WMA or hypokinesis, RV dilation (RV:LV ratio >1), interventricular septal bowing, IVC collapse, “D-sign”: septal flattening, “McConnell’s sign”: RV free wall akinesia w/ normal RV apex motion (77% Sn, 94% Sp for acute PE)




• Tamponade: effusion, RA collapse in systole (earliest sonographic sign; high sensitivity), RV collapse in diastole (high specificity), respirophasic variation in mitral inflow velocity by > 25%), interventricular septal bowing, plethoric IVC (no ↓ w/ inspiration)




• ACS and associated mechanical complications: regional WMA, septal/free wall rupture, acute MR, LV thrombus




• Stress (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy: LV apical ballooning and akinesis/hypokinesis; Heart failure: depressed EF, RV/LV hypertrophy and/or dilation




• Diastolic dysfunction: LA enlargement, E/e’ >14, LVH ( )




• Constrictive pericarditis: thickened or hyperechoic pericardium, abnormal septal motion, respiratory variation in ventricular size, dilated IVC




• Cardiac amyloid: biatrial enlargement, increased LV and RV wall thickening, valvular thickening, diastolic dysfunction, paradoxical LFLG AS, strain imaging with reduced global longitudinal strain and apical sparing

topics.title: Heart Failure

panels.title: ACUTE DECOMPENSATED HEART FAILURE MANAGEMENT – FLOOR/SDU

topics.text:
BASIC FRAMEWORK


Diagnosis of heart failure vs cardiomyopathy (CM)




• Heart failure is a clinical diagnosis – requires signs/symptoms of volume overload (e.g. orthopnea, leg swelling, crackles, ↑JVP) attributable to a structural or functional impairment in ventricular ejection or filling




• Heart failure ≠ cardiomyopathy – a CM is an abnormality in myocardial structure or function, usually visualized by TTE (does not require signs/symptoms of volume overload)




Classifications of heart failure




• LVEF classes: HFpEF (LVEF >50%), HFmrEF (‘mildly reduced’ EF; LVEF 41-49%), HFrEF (LVEF ≤40%), HFimpEF (‘improved’ EF; previous LVEF ≤40% and a follow-up measurement of LFEF > 40%)




• ACC/AHA Stage and NYHA Functional Class (see Figure)











Identifying underlying etiology







Category




Cardiomyopathy etiologies




Most common




ischemic, hypertensive, valvular




Metabolic




diabetic, nutritional deficiency (e.g. beriberi)




High-output




septic, peripartum, hyperthyroid, anemia, liver failure, Paget’s, AV shunts




Toxins/drugs




alcohol, cocaine/amphetamines, chemotherapy, immune checkpoint inhibitors




Infectious




HIV, coxsackie, echovirus, EBV, CMV, Lyme, Chagas disease, tuberculosis




Infiltrative




amyloidosis (ATTR or AL), hemochromatosis, sarcoidosis, Löffler’s




Genetic




hypertrophic cardiomyopathy/HOCM, ARVC, familial neuromuscular disorders, glycogen storage disorders, LVNC




Inflammatory




connective tissue diseases, giant cell myocarditis




Other




pulmonary (cor pulmonale), stress-induced (Takotsubo), tachyarrhythmia-induced, pericardial disease (e.g. constrictive pericarditis, pericardial effusion), radiation, carcinoid, idiopathic





NOTE: CM can be additional defined as ‘dilated,’ ‘hypertrophic,’ and ‘restrictive’ based on morphology/structure seen on imaging




Workup




• Initial workup: signs/sxs of volume overload, troponin, NTproBNP, ECG, tele, CXR, TTE




• Ischemic CM workup: family hx, smoking hx, lipid panel, A1c, see Non-Invasive Testing and Cardiac Catherization




• Non-ischemic CM workup: family hx, med hx, substance use hx, tox screen, β-hCG, iron studies, SPEP/UPEP/FLC, TSH, HIV, ANA




• Extended workup (when applicable): chest CT, cardiac MRI, RHC, endomyocardial biopsy, PYP scan, viral serology panel, Lyme serologies, T. cruzi serologies, ACE level, thiamine/carnitine/selenium, genetic testing, antimyosin Ab




Management of heart failure




• Treat the underlying causes of (1) cardiomyopathy and (2) decompensation triggers




• Basic elements of treatment: diuresis, afterload reduction, consideration of device/advanced therapies




• Guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT):






◦ HFrEF/HFmrEF/HFimpEF = BB, ACEi/ARB/ARNi, MRA, SGLT2i




◦ HFpEF = MRA, SGLT2i





2022 ACC/AHA HF Guidelines:




Circ 2022;145:895









• Cardiomyopathy-specific interventions: ischemic = PCI, CABG; valvular = TAVR, MitraClip, other valve interventions; tachyarrhytmia-induced = ablation, PPM, CRT; ATTR amyloid = tafamadis ↓TTR deposition (NEJM 2018;379:1007), acoramadis, vutrisiran; sarcoid = prednisone, steroid-sparing IST




CONSIDERATIONS FOR SELECT CARDIOMYOPATHIES

Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM) (Circulation 2024;149 :e1239)




Characteristics: LV and/or RV hypertrophy ± LVOT dynamic obstruction (HOCM), diastolic dysfxn, ischemia, MR; risk of SCD




Exam: SEM at LLSB/apex that augments with Valsalva or on standing (due to ↓preload); S2 paradox split, S4




Dx: ECG (prominent voltages w/ depol abnormalities, large Q waves in inferior/lateral leads, LAD, negative T waves in V2-V4 (apical HCM), TTE (LVH >15mm, SAM of MV, outflow tract gradient +/- provocative test), cMRI (late gadolinium enhancement [LGE] = fibrosis) Clinical genetic testing (mutation in ~70%) helpful for family screening; not useful for dx or risk stratification




Tx: avoid volume depletion or high dose vasodilators (may worsen obstruction); phenylephrine is pressor of choice if no response to IVF bolus for HoTN (↑afterload, stents open LVOT). Activity restriction, meds (disopyramide, BB > verapamil). Cardiac myosin inhibitors (e.g. aficamten, mavacamten) if LVEF ≥ 55% (VALOR-HCM); septal ablation or surgical myectomy if medically refractory, ICD ifhigh risk




Risk factors for SCD/VT: prior VT/SCD/unexplained syncope; FHx of SCD in 1° relative; massive LVH (>30mm); NSVT on Holter; abnormal BP response to exercise; burden of LGE on cMRI; h/o suspected cardiac syncope; EF<50%







• Amyloidosis (AL, TTR): HF + amyloid findings (e.g. renal), low voltage ECG, thick LV/RV on TTE, LGE in subendocardium on cMRI




• Hemochromatosis: hereditary or secondary, ECG with SVT, dilated LV on TTE, iron overload on T2 protocol of cMRI




• Sarcoidosis: ECG with atypical infarct pattern or block, patchy enhancement of basal and LV walls on cMRI




ACUTE DECOMPENSATED HEART FAILURE MANAGEMENT – FLOOR/SDU
Identify hemodynamic profile and triage accordingly (JACC2019;74:1966)






• Warm vs Cold: consider AMS, lactate, cool extremities, narrow pulse press




• Dry vs Wet: presence vs absence of congestion




• Evaluate for pulmonary congestion on exam. Pulm edema may be absent on CXR due to lymphatic compensation (Chest2004;125:669)




• Majority of HFrEF and HFpEF pts will be warm and wet




• See ‘Right Ventricular Failure’ for special considerations for patients with primarily right-sided heart disease











History




• Identify decompensation triggers: Mnemonic FAILURE – F = forgot meds, A = arrhythmia/anemia/afterload, I = infection/ischemia, L = lifestyle (salty diet), U = upregulation of cardiac output (e.g. pregnancy, hyperthyroid), R = renal failure, E = embolism. Other triggers: progression of CM, inadequate diuretic dose, meds (NSAIDs, steroids, CCB, anthracyclines), toxins (EtOH), new/worsened valve




• HF history (prior CM dx, dry weight, last NTproBNP, last TTE/EF, prior ischemic w/u, outpt cardiologist), accurate PAML, social/fam hx




Admission considerations




• Admission orders: tele, 2g Na-restricted diet, daily standing weights, strict I/Os, DVT ppx, (SDU only) electrolyte replenishment scales




• SDU admission indications: EF <25%, NTproBNP ≥ 2,500, arrhythmia-induced HF. Black & Latinx pts w/ HF are less likely to be admitted to cardiology services, contributing to racial inequities in HF outcomes (Circ Heart Fail 2019;12:e006214)




• Avoid: CCB (esp. non-dihydropyridines), NSAIDs, flecainide




• Check NT-proBNP (& weight) on admission. ADHF unlikely if NT-proBNP <300 (NPV 98%), likely if >450 (>900 if age >50) (Am J Cardiol 2005;95;948). Difficult to interpret in CKD/dialysis. May be falsely low in obesity, HFpEF




• Screen for and treat iron deficiency in all HF pts independent of Hgb (JACCHF2019;7:36)




◦ Dx: ferritin <100 or ferritin <300 + TSat <20% (JACC2017;70:776)




◦ Tx: replete with IV iron (JACC2018;71:782) to ↓sx, ↑functional capacity, and possibly improve outcomes (NEJM 2023;389:975)




Early/acute management




• Diuresis: ↓CVP, PCWP to optimize Starling curve mechanics & relieve sx (NEJM2017;377:1964;JACC2020;75:1178)




◦ Initial tx: IV loop (furosemide, torsemide, bumetanide), start w/ 20-40mg IV furosemide if diuretic-naïve otherwise start w/ 2-2.5x home dose (IV/PO). No difference b/w continuous gtt vs bolus (NEJM2011;364:797).See Advanced Diuresis




◦ Refractory diuresis: add metolazone 2.5-5mg (or chlorothiazide 500mg IV) administered 30min before loop diuretic. May need RHC to clarify hemodynamics or inotropes to augment diuresis. Acetazolamide (500mg daily), as well as dapagliflozin (10mg daily), may also augment successful decongestion (NEJM 2022;387:1185; EHJ 2023;44:2966). Step-up pharmacologic therapy superior to RRT in the setting of cardiorenal syndrome (NEJM2012;367:2296)




◦ Worsening renal function: Common occurrence. Mild-mod “Cr bumps” likely benign, should not necessarily preclude further diuresis if pt still congested (Circ2018;137:2016)




◦ Endpoints: target resolution of signs/symptoms of congestion. Daily weights, hemoconcentration, lung and JVP POCUS are useful adjuncts to ensure diuresis to euvolemia. B-lines on lung US portend ↑risk of HF admissions/death (EHJ 2016;37:1244)




• If acute pulmonary edema, NIPPV may improve mortality and reduce need for intubation (Annals2010;152:590)




• Vasodilators: arterial/venous dilation can relieve symptoms by ↓afterload, ↓PCWP. Consider esp. in severe HTN, acute MR or AR




◦ Floor: isosorbide dinitrate, hydralazine, nitropaste, captopril; SDU/CCU: nitro gtt, nitroprusside gtt (caution if uncorrected CAD)




• Home GDMT continuation: if not in cardiogenic shock or new AKI, continue ACEi/ARB/ARNi and βB (at fractionated dose) during ADHF (but do not newly initiate βB) (EHJ 2009;30:2186). Hold SGLT2i as it may preclude procedure




Guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT)




• HFrEF, HFmrEF (+/- HFimpEF): prioritize initiation of low-dose quadruple GDMT prior to d/c




◦ Beta-blockers (BB): initiate BB (carvedilol, metoprolol succ., bisoprolol) (COPERNICUS; MERIT-HF).Caution if recent inotropes




◦ RAAS inhibitors: if renal fxn stable, initiate/titrate ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) (PARADIGM-HF;PIONEER-HF),secondlineACEi/ARB (CONSENSUS;CHARM). Switch to ARNI from ACEi/ARB if no C.I./cost concerns, 36h washout period for ACEi prior to ARNI




◦ MRA: initiate spironolactone or eplerenone if CrCl>30 (EMPHASIS-HF;RALES). Watch for rebound hyperK after de-escalation of diuretics (check K, Cr within 72h of discharge)




◦ SGLT2i: dapaglifozin and empagliflozin reduce mortality and HF admissions regardless of DM (DAPA-HF; EMPEROR-Reduced)




◦ Guidance for GDMT in advanced CKD: JACCHF2019;7:371




◦ GDMT dosing - AHA/ACC/HFSA 2022 Guidelines (Circ 2022;145:895)

• HFpEF: improve volume overload with diuretics, treat comorbidities (DM, HTN, AF), add GDMT




◦ SGLT2i found to ↓CV death/hospitalizations in pts with EF >40% (EMPEROR-Preserved, DELIVER)




◦ Consider spironolactone if normal renal fxn/K, ↓CV death/admits in N/S Am. sites in TOPCAT (Circ2015;131:34)




◦ No proven benefit to BB (EHJ2018;39:26), ACEi (PEP-CHF), ARNi (PARAGON-HF), ARB (CHARM-Preserved;I-PRESERVE)




◦ New options: finerenone (nonsteroidal MRA) (NEJM 2024;391:1475), semaglutide (GLP1ra) (NEJM 2023;389:2221)




• ICD indicated if: ischemic CM w/ EF ≤30 or ≤35% w/ NYHA II-III; CRT if: EF ≤35% & prolonged QRS ± LBBB & some w/ EF ≤50% (see Cardiac Devices: PPM/ICD & guidelines for specifics:JACC2013;61:e6;EHJ2016;37:2129)




Pre-discharge optimization
Pre-discharge optimization




• Document d/c weight and NTproBNP, appt in HF Transitions Clinic, referral to cardiac rehab




• Optimization of GDMT as above




• Diuretic plan: determine maintenance oral diuretic dose and provide specific instructions for taking additional rescue doses. Consider inpatient observation on maintenance dose and decide if needs K replacement.




CARDIOGENIC SHOCK – CCU
• Stages: A. “At risk” B. “Beginning”=HDUS pt w/o hypoperfusion (e.g. oliguria, ↑lactate, ↑ Cr.), C. “Classic”=signs of hypoperfusion (HoTN maybe absent), D. “Deteriorating”=no improvement to initial therapy, E. “Extremis” (JSCAI 2021:1:1)




• Evaluation: ECG, troponin to r/o acute MI. TTE to exclude tamponade/mechanical lesions/contraindications to MCS




• Monitoring: A-line, consider PA catheter for inotropes/pressors and MVO2 monitoring




Immediate Management:




• If c/f acute MI, activate cath lab for PCI (only intervention proven to improve outcomes in cardiogenic shock) (NEJM1999;341:625)




• ). Escalating inotropes/pressors a/w poor outcomes. Evidence for early initiation of MCS




• Stabilize MAP with norepinephrine PRN prior to obtaining PA catheter to guide tailored therapy




Tailored Therapy: uses invasive hemodynamic monitoring (i.e., PAC) to guide medical therapy. See Pulmonary Artery Catheterization.




• Goals: tissue perfusion (↑CO, MAP), decongestion (↓CVP, PCWP), ventricular unloading (minimize myocardial O2 demand)




◦ Preload: LVEDV ∝ LVEDP ≈ PCWP; goal PCWP 14-18, PAD 16-20, CVP 8-12 → diuresis, UF with RRT




◦ Afterload: wall stress ∝ MAP (Laplace’s law); SVR = (MAP - CVP)/CO; goal MAP >60, SVR <800-1200




▪ Vasodilators: captopril, hydralazine, nitroprusside, TNG, isosorbide dinitrate




▪ Vasopressors: ↑afterload, sometimes needed to ↑MAP in mixed shock or to counteract vasodilatory effect of inodilators




◦ Contractility: ∝ CO for given preload/afterload; goal CO>4, CI >2.0-2.2, MVO2 >65




▪ Dobutamine (inodilator): β1>β2 agonist (↑production of cAMP); initial dose 0.5-1 mcg/kg/min




• Watch for tachycardia, ↑ventricular response to AF, arrhythmias, ischemia, HoTN, tachyphylaxis in infusions >24-48h




▪ Milrinone (inodilator): PDE-3 inhibitor (↓breakdown of cAMP); initial dose 0.125 mcg/kg/min




• Watch for tachycardia, arrhythmias, ischemia, HoTN. Compared to dobutamine, milrinone has longer half-life, greater pulmonary vasodilatation, slightly less chronotropy




• Preferred in patients w/ RV failure. Renally cleared. Often choice for home inotrope for palliative therapy




▪ Epi (inopressor): use if severe HoTN often in combo with inodilators. Watch for arrhythmias, end-organ hypoperfusion




◦ Advanced: consideration of need for MCS or transplant to improve systemic perfusion; see Mechanical Circulatory Support

topics.title: Right Ventricular Failure

panels.title: INTUBATION AND MECHANICAL VENTILATION (Curr Heart Fail Rep 2012;9:228)

topics.text:
PATHOPHYSIOLOGY AND ETIOLOGIES (NEJM 2023;388:1111)


• Normal RV function: governed by systemic venous return, PA pressure, pericardial compliance, and native contractility of the RV free wall and interventricular septum (where RV and LV are “tethered”)




◦ The RV is coupled to the high-compliance, low-resistance pulm circulation → RV ejects blood at lower pressure compared to LV → RV is more afterload sensitive than LV. RV can adapt to changes in volume > pressure.




• Acute RV Failure: RV & LV interdependent → failure of RV → failure of LV via: (1) decreased LV preload, as RV output = LV preload & (2) septal bowing into LV, causing diastolic impairment (“Diastolic Ventricular Interaction”)




◦ ↑RV afterload (e.g. PE, hypoxemia, acidemia), ↑RV preload (e.g. L→R shunt or TV disease), or ↓RV contractility (e.g. MI, myocarditis) all lead to increased RV wall stress & resultant ischemia -> “death spiral”




• Chronic RV Failure: gradual ↑RV afterload (e.g. from pulmonary hypertension / pulmonic stenosis / tricuspid regurgitation)





















CLINICAL FEATURES AND WORKUP (Circ 2018;137:e578-e622)
• Exam: ↑JVP, Kussmaul’s sign (↑JVP with inspiration), peripheral edema, RV heave, pulsatile liver, split S2, new TR murmur




• EKG: RAD, R:S amplitude >1 in V1, p-wave > 2.5mm in inferior leads (P pulmonale), S1Q3T3 (RV strain in PE), atrial arrhythmias




• Labs: NT-proBNP, troponin, also ↑Cr and LFTs secondary to venous congestion (LFTs may be normal in chronic RV failure)




• Imaging: PA/lateral CXR; chest CT → RV/LV ratio >0.9 suggests RV strain




• Echo: measure RV size/fxn/pressure to elucidate etiology. Aortic root, LA, RV should be ~1:1:1 in size (PSL view). RV should be < LV in size (Apical 4Ch view). RVEF based on displacement of base towards apex, correlates with TAPSE = tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (normal ≥ 17 mm; reflects apex-to-base shortening). RVSP calculated from TR jet, correlates w/ RHC but can vary within 10mmHg (esp w/ lung disease, PPV)




• RHC w/ placement of PA line: gold standard for measurement of ventricular filling pressures, CO, PA pressures




◦ Assessments of RV function – CVP/PCWP ratio: normal = 0.5, ↑ is sign of RV dysfunction; PAPi: (PAs – PAd)/CVP <0.9 = RV failure, for pts w/ VAD < 1.85 = RV failure; RV stroke work index: (mPAP – CVP) x (CI/HR) x 0.0136 (normal 8-12 g/m/beat/m2)




MANAGEMENT (Circ 2018;137:e578)
• Treat reversible causes (e.g. pericardial disease, RVMI, PE, hypoxemia, infections)




• Preload (CVP goal 8-12mmHg): both hypo- and hypervolemia can ↓CO




◦ Volume responsive (PE, RVMI): judicious IVF (0.5-1L) in absence of CVP elevation (goal CVP 10-14 in RVMI)




◦ Volume overload: IV diuresis to ↓RV pressures, ↓functional TR, and improve LV CO; consider CRRT if refractory to diuresis




• Afterload:




◦ Systemic: if pt hypotensive, start pressors – do not tolerate HoTN as propagates RV death spiral (↓CPP); Goal MAP>65 & MAP>mPAP (EHJ Acute CV Care 2022;11:77) no clinical data regarding pressor of choice, but often choose vasopressin or norepinephrine (vaso affects PVR less than norepi) (Crit Care Med 2007;35:2037)




◦ Pulmonary: remove factors that ↑pulm vasc tone (e.g. hypoxemia, acidemia). Consider pulm vasodilators if evidence of PAH (inhaled>oral to deliver vasodilators to ventilated vascular beds)




▪ Types: iNO, prostacyclin agonists (epoprostenol (Veletri), inhaled or IV), endothelin antagonists (e.g. bosentan, ambrisentan), nitric oxide enhancers (e.g. PDE-5 inhibitors: sildenafil, tadalafil)




• Contractility: milrinone (↓RV afterload by pulm vasodilation but ↑HoTN risk); epinephrine (↑RV contractility, ↑MAP). In RVMI, important to revascularize urgently as inotropes can exacerbate ischemia.




• Devices: if refractory RVF, consider RV MCS and/or biventricular support (ProtekDuo, Impella RP, VA-ECMO)




INTUBATION AND MECHANICAL VENTILATION (Curr Heart Fail Rep 2012;9:228)
• RV preload is “extrathoracic” and afterload is “intrathoracic” → intubation/PPV ↑ PVR & RV afterload→↑ RV dilation→“death spiral”




• Mech vent/NIPPV in RV failure precipitate risk for hemodynamic collapse & cardiac arrest; trial of HFNC for hypoxemic respiratory failure preferred prior to MV/NIPPV given minimal effect on RV afterload.




◦ Drugs commonly used in intubation (BZDs, propofol, muscle relaxants) → tendency towards vasodilation and negative inotropy → decreased venous return → decreased RV/LV preload → systemic hypoTN → propagates “death spiral”




◦ Consider rapid sequence intubation w/ hemodynamically stable induction agents (ketamine/etomidate >> propofol for induction) & push dose epinephrine (5-20mcg) or phenylephrine if emergent intubation; have norepi in line anticipating hypotension.




• Vent management: prevent hypoxemia & hypercarbia (↑PVR), consider moderate TV (~8cc/kg), low PEEP (<8 cm H2O), and moderate plateau pressure goal (<30 mmHg) to help minimize RV afterload




RIGHT VENTRICULAR MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION (ACC/AHA: Circ 2013;127:e362)
• EKG: check R-sided ECG leads in pts with inferior STEMI (10-15% have RV involvement)




◦ 1mm STE in V4R → 88% Sn, 78% Sp in inferior STEMI; STE III>II suggests RCA > LCx and RVMI




◦ High-grade AV block seen in ~50% of pts with RVMI




• Management: pts with RVMI may initially benefit from fluid bolus; caution w/ TNG (↓preload) & BB

MECHANICAL CIRCULATORY SUPPORT (MCS) (JACC HF 2020; 8(11):879 ; Heart Int 2022; 16(1):37)
).







Device




Indications




Support Provided




Considerations*




Management




Complications




IABP




(intra-




aortic




balloon




bump)




- Refractory heart failure (bridge to durable MCS or transplant, bridge- to-bridge)




- Refractory ischemia




- Cardiogenic shock or massive PE




- Refractory malignant




arrhythmias




- Support during




high-risk




procedures:




◦ Complex PCI




◦ Ablation of ventricular arrhythmias




◦ Percutaneous valve repair




- Acute allograft failure




- Mechanism: balloon inflation/deflation timed with cardiac cycle; ↓LV afterload (deflation),




↑coronary perfusion (inflation)




- Minimal LV-only support (0.3-0.5




L/min)




- Amount of support determined by balloon cycle per # of cardiac cycles (1:1>1:2>1:3)




- Requires native contractility and




stable rhythm




- Bedside insertion but often placed in cath lab under fluoroscopy




- Does not always require AC (no




AC need when at 1:1)




- No ↓mortality in cardiogenic shock (IABP-SHOCK II)




- Prevents mobility




- Check CXR daily (tip 1-4cm below aortic knob)




- Check waveform twice daily




- Daily pulse checks




- Wean by ↓ ratio (then




return to 1:1, stop AC, pull)




- Limb ischemia




- Vascular injury




- Thromboembolism




- Thrombocytopenia




- Bleeding




- Infection




- Balloon leak/rupture (STAT c/s to attending and vascular surg)




Impella




- Mechanism: axial-flow continuous pump; unloads ventricle




- Partial LV-only support




(LV→aorta):




Cath lab (percutaneous) placement: Impella 2.5 (2.5 L/min), Impella CP




(3.5 L/min)




OR placement: Impella 5.0 (5 L/min) or 5.5 (6.5 L/min)




- Partial RV-only support (IVC→PA) Impella RP (>4 L/min)




- Amount of support determined by pump power [P1 (low) to P9 (high]




- Requires AC (purge ± systemic); purge solution can be heparin or bicarbonate




- Upgrade to Impella 5.5 when able (fewer complications, allows pt




mobilization)




- Days to weeks of support




- ↓ mortality in cardiogenic shock due to MI (DanGer Shock)




- Controversial benefit over IABP




- Check daily hemolysis markers




- Daily limited TTE (to check position)




- Check suction events (can indicate ↓preload, RV failure, thrombosis, mispositioning)




- Check telemetry (ventricular arrhythmias may indicate device migration)

arrhythmias

VA-




ECMO




- Mechanism: heart-lung bypass device




- Full bi-ventricular support (4-10 L/min) + oxygenation & CO2 clearance




- Bedside and urgent insertion possible




- Days to weeks of support




- Often requires Impella for LV venting (prevents complications such as pulmonary edema)




See ECMO




Durable




VAD




- Bridge to transplant




- Bridge to candidacy




- Destination therapy




- Bridge to recovery (LV unloading can be therapeutic)




- Mechanism: continuous centrifugal- flow intracorporeal pump designed for long-term out-of-hospital use




- Full LV-only support (LV→aorta)




at 10 L/min

- HeartMate 3 (HM3) device is most utilized (HeartMate II and HeartWare HVAD now discontinued, but remain in patients with implantation prior to removal off the market)

warfarin

INDICATIONS FOR HEART TRANSPLANT (CURR OPIN NEPHROL HYPERTENS 2025;34:16)
Advanced HF refractory to therapy, defined as: (1) cardiogenic shock requiring inotrope or MCS, or (2) NYHA class IV sx refractory to maximal therapy alongside low HF prognosis score or poor CPET results, or (3) refractory life-threatening arrhythmias

panels.title: OBTAINING PA LINE NUMBERS ON AM ROUNDS

runs.t: OBTAINING PA LINE NUMBERS ON AM ROUNDS

topics.text:
OVERVIEW
• Indications: PA catheter (PAC) for tailored therapy; diagnose (1) undifferentiated shock (2) cardiogenic vs. non-cardiogenic pulm edema;






(3) LV vs RV failure; (4) etiology of PH; (5) L→ R shunting; (6) valve disease; (7) pericardial disease




• Efficacy: controversial - ESCAPE trial (JAMA2005;294:1625) showed no mortality benefit to empiric use of PAC in pts w/ ADHF off inotropes. Recent observational study (JACC Heart Fail 2020:8:11) mortality benefit for cardiogenic shock. PACs are still guideline-recommended in carefully selected patients (e.g. pts w/ MCS) (Circulation 2022;145:e895)




• Line course: central vein (IJ/fem)→SVC/IVC→RA→RV→PA→distal pulmonary arteriole




V E NO US W AV E F O RM S (CVP/PCWP)




• a wave: atrial contraction; coincides with the QRS complex (on CVP tracing)




• c wave: bowing of TV into atrium during ventricular contraction; more visible in 1st degree AVB




• x descent: atrial relaxation (early x descent), downward movement of TV (late x descent)




• v wave: passive atrial filling (venous return) when TV/MV closed; coincides with T wave




• y descent: rapid atrial emptying following opening of the TV (ventricular diastole)




• Sample waveforms available in J Clin Monit Comput 2022;36:5











OBTAINING PA LINE NUMBERS ON AM ROUNDS
O BT AINI NG PA L I NE N UM BE RS O N AM R O UN DS




1) Position patient supine with head-of-bed between 0-60°






2) Align transducer with mid-axillary line (4th intercostal space)




3) Zero transducer to air & assess waveform for dampness




4) Record PA systolic, PA diastolic, PA mean, CVP, & line position




5) Open the PA catheter balloon port & remove 1.5cc air




6) Inject 1.5cc air slowly until PCWP waveform observed (use minimum air required to ↓ risk of PA infarction/rupture) & record PCWP (limit balloon inflation <10 seconds)




7) Release safety syringe & allow balloon to deflate passively; verify balloon deflated by visualizing the PA waveform




8) Troubleshooting: CXR to evaluate position (obtained daily)




a. Arrhythmia: catheter may be in RVOT; consider repositioning




b. Dampened waveform: kinked tubing, air/thrombus, or catheter tip against vessel wall; flush and/or withdraw catheter




c. No PCWP tracing: catheter tip is not far enough, balloon has ruptured, or catheter is coiled in RV




d. Continuous PCWP: catheter tip is advanced too far (“overwedged”)




e. mvO2 resembles arterial O2: catheter tip is advanced too far













C AL CUL AT ING H E M O DY NAM I C P ARAM E T E RS




• Normal: “rule of 5s” → RA 5, RV 25/5, PA 25/10, PCWP 10, LV 125/10




• Cardiac output: TD better predicts mortality (JAMACardiol2017:10:10)




◦ Fick = VO2 / (13.4 * Hgb * [SpO2 – MvO2]) [nml: 4-8 L/min]




▪ VO2 ≈ 250 ml/min OR 3*wt(kg) OR 125*BSA




◦ Thermodilution (TD): temp change (measured by thermistor) is proportional to LV CO (inaccurate if: severe TR, intracardiac shunt, very low CO)




• Cardiac index = CO/BSA [nl: 2.2-4.2 L/min/m2] (nl ↓ w/ age)




• SVR = (MAP-CVP) / CO x 80 [nl: 700-1200 dynes*s*cm5]




• PVR = (mPAP-PCWP) / CO [nl: <2 Woods units]




• PAPi = (PASP – PADP) / RAP [PAPi < 0.9 → severe RV dysfxn]

HEMODYNAMIC CONSIDERATIONS
• All quantitative pressure measurements (especially PCWP) should be made at end-expiration (when intrathoracic pressure is zero)




◦ Spontaneous respiration: RA & PCWP ↑ with expiration → measure from the higher a waves (“patient = peak”)




◦ Positive pressure ventilation: RA & PCWP ↓ with expiration → measure from the lower a waves (“vent = valley”)




• Measure RA & PCWP at end-diastole (i.e. just before the c wave)




• Correlate PCWP with PA diastolic pressure; if well correlated, can trend PAd as proxy for PCWP (allowing for less frequent wedging)




CLINICAL CONSIDERATIONS
• Placement: usually through RIJ Cordis. Advance ONLY with balloon inflated. Deflate balloon when withdrawing and at ALL other times.




.




◦ Cath lab if: severe PH (>70mmHg), large RV/RA, LBBB, PPM/ICD <6mo, temp wire, severe TR, prosthetic TV/PV, femoral access




• Contraindications: absolute – insertion site infection, RVAD, RA/RV mass/thrombosis, mechanical TV/PV, endocarditis (TV/PV)




• Position: on CXR, should be in middle 1/3 of the chest bilaterally; ability to wedge more important than CXR position




• Complications: infection, bleeding, thrombosis, PTX, arrythmia (PVC, NSVT, VT), RBBB, CHB, valve trauma, PA rupture (place patient on side with the catheter “bleeding side down”, order STAT CXR, CBC, coags, CT surgery consult), RV perforation, pulm infarct, PE, catheter knotting (difficult removal), balloon rupture & embolization

• Types: single chamber (RA or RV lead), dual chamber (RA + RV leads), biventricular (RV + coronary sinus ± RA leads)




• PPM: sense/pace the RA & RV to treat bradyarrhythmias (see tables for nomenclature and common modes)

topics.title: Valvular Heart Disease
topics.text:
AORTIC STENOSIS
• Etiology: degenerative calcific AS (age-related; precursor is aortic sclerosis; most common cause >70yo), bicuspid valve (most common cause <70yo), rheumatic heart disease (RHD; often w/ leaflet fusion, concurrent MV dz), radiation




• Clinical Manifestations: most important determinant of prognosis = sxs: 50% mortality at 5y if angina, 3y if syncope, 2y if HF




◦ Angina: ↑afterload → ↑LV pressures → LVH → ↑O2 demand → supply-demand mismatch w/ exertion or tachycardia




◦ Syncope: caused by exercise-induced vasodilation w/ fixed ability to augment CO due to stenosis




◦ Heart failure (dyspnea): LVH → diastolic dysfunction (systolic dysfunction is a late finding)




◦ Acquired vWF def: 20% of severe AS, can worsen bleeding from GI AVMs “Heyde syndrome” (NEJM 2012;367:1954)




• Diagnosis:




◦ Physical exam: harsh crescendo-decrescendo murmur at RUSB radiating to carotids. Signs of severe AS: late-peaking murmur (long ejection time), delayed carotid upstroke (pulsus parvus et tardus), soft or paradoxical split S2, diminished murmur (low flow)




◦ TTE: measure mean (not peak) gradient, valve area, & peak jet velocity; assess EF as ↓ flow →↓ gradient confounds severity




• Severe AS: peak AV velocity ≥4m/s, mean AV pressure grad ≥40mmHg, or AV area (AVA) ≤1cm2 (ACC/AHA: Circ 2021;143:e35)




◦ ECG: LVH, LAE, LAFB, LBBB




◦ Exercise stress testing: recommended in asymptomatic severe AS to assess for symptoms; do not perform in pts w/ sx




◦ Low-flow/low-gradient AS: severity underestimated in reduced EF as ↓ flow →↓ gradient. Subsets distinguished by flow (low-




flow: SVi <35 mL/m2), gradient (low-gradient: <40mmHg), LVEF, and dobutamine stress TTE (DSE) (Circ 2011;124:739)




▪ True LF/LG AS: low EF, flow, & gradient; confirm w/ DSE Vmax>4m/s or gradient>40mmHg w/ AVA<1cm2; poor outcomes




▪ Pseudosevere AS: a normal valve w/ low measured AVA in the setting of low EF; due to flow-dependent AVA estimation and decreased ability of weakened ventricle to fully open aortic valve; confirm w/ DSE with improved AVA >1cm2




▪ Paradoxical LF/LG AS: preserved EF, yet low-flow and low-gradient; poor outcomes (Circulation 2013;128:1781)




• Natural History: highly variable, but on average, AVA ↓ ~0.1 cm2/yr & mean gradient ↑8mmHg/yr (JACC 1989;13:545). Patients with bicuspid valves, advanced age, & those with severe leaflet calcification are at risk for more rapid progression




• Aortic Valve Replacement (AVR) (J Am Soc Echo 2018;31:117): indications based on: symptoms, severity (TTE criteria), LVEF




◦ Symptomatic, severe AS (Stage D): prompt AVR indicated due to risk of sudden death




◦ Asymptomatic, severe AS (Stage C): AVR appropriate if: LVEF<50%; symptoms provoked with exercise testing; or undergoing other cardiac surgery. For patients with asymptomatic very severe AS (AVA ≤0.75cm2), early surgery may have mortality benefit (NEJM 2020;382:111). For asymptomatic severe AS, early TAVR may reduce unplanned CV hospitalization (EARLY TAVR).




◦ Low-flow, low-gradient AS: true LF/LG = AVR indicated, paradoxical = AVR if symptomatic, pseudosevere = AVR not indicated




◦ Bioprosthetic vs Mechanical: if contraindications to AC with VKA, must offer bioprosthetic; if pt <50 years of age without contraindications to AC, SAVR w/ mechanical valve recommended (COR 1; Circulation 2021;143:35); if >65 yrs of age, bioprosthetic recommended (COR 2a); 50-65 years of age require shared decision making




◦ SAVR vs TAVR for bioprosthetic: pts <65yr, SAVR recommended d/t increased durability; >80yr TAVR recommended




◦ 65-80 yrs of age: depends on surgical risk (STS-PROMscore), concomitant heart/vascular disease, valvular/vascular anatomy that is amenable to TAVR (Circulation 2021;143:35)




◦ TAVR is recommended for those at extreme surgical risk (compared to medical therapy, PARTNER); noninferior to SAVR in those at high (NEJM 2011;364:2187), intermediate (PARTNER 2), & low surgical risk (PARTNER 3). Valve-in- valve TAVR may additionally be beneficial in pts with surgical bioprosthetic AV failure (JACC 2017;69:2253)




◦ TAVR Evaluation: c/s structural cardiology, cardiac surgery. Obtain TTE, TAVR-protocol CT, dental clearance (Panorex)




◦ TAVR Complications: Valve: embolization, paravalvular leak; Stroke: embolic (first 48h), ischemic/hemorrhagic; Conduction:




HAVB requiring PPM (Major RF: baseline RBBB, need for pacing or HAVB s/p TAVR; Minor: h/o AF, valve oversized >15%; Card Fail Rev 2021; 7:e12); Bleeding; Access site complication; Hemodynamics: dynamic LVOT obstruction due to LVH (“suicide LV”), HTN (sudden ↓ in obstruction after TAVR), hypotension (d/t ↓preload), tamponade (perforation, usually immediate); AKI




• Medical Management: AS is a surgical disease & medical management is only utilized for treatment of sx




◦ Treat HTN: reduce the “double load” on the ventricle. In theory, ACE-I beneficial for LV fibrosis; however, no optimal regimen exists because anti-hypertensives can lead to hemodynamic issues. Bottom line: start low and go slow




◦ Control volume status: operate within a narrow preload range, prone to underfilling (low preload) & overfilling (volume overload)




• Anticoagulation after Valve Replacement:




◦ Bridging UFH or LMWH if AC interrupted only in mechanical MV or mechanical AV with RFs (Class I),




◦ RFs: AF, LV dysfxn, prior VTE, hypercoag, older generaction mechanical AVR (Circ 2021;143:e35)




◦ Bleeding risk: mechanical > bioprosthetic (likely AC related). Reoperation risk: bioprosthetic > mechanical




◦ TAVR: ASA monotherapy non-inferior to DAPT for thrombotic events & associated with less bleeding (NEJM 2020;383:1447)




◦ If need AC for AF, DOACs similar outcome after TAVR, not approved for valvular MS (moderate+) (JAHA 2021;11:e023561)
