topics.text:
TYPES OF TRANSPLANT




Allogeneic Transplant




Autologous Transplant




Definition




Transplant of non-self (donor) hematopoietic cells




Transplant of self (patient) hematopoietic cells




Goals




Reconstitute hematopoiesis after conditioning chemo and graft-versus-tumor (GVT) effect to kill malignant cells. Also used for bone marrow failure syndromes. Always curative intent.




Reconstitute hematopoiesis after high-dose




chemotherapy. Intent generally curative except in plasma cell disorders, where goal is to prolong remission




Indications




↑risk AML (40-60% 5YS), ALL (40-50% 5YS), MDS (45% 5YS), ↑risk myelofibrosis, TKI-resistant CML,




relapsed lymphoma, aplastic anemia, thalassemia, sickle cell disease, primary immunodeficiency (SCID), inborn errors of metabolism




1st relapsed lymphomas (40-50% 5YS), MM (35% 5YS); relapsed Waldenström, AL amyloidosis, select solid tumors (germ cell, neuroblastoma, Ewing sarcoma), autoimmune disease (MS, SS, Crohns, SLE)




Source of cells




Mostly peripheral blood, but some centers use more bone marrow given lower risk of chronic GVHD. Umbilical cord blood is occasionally used




Usually peripheral blood given less invasive harvest, more rapid engraftment




Time to engraftment




14-28 days (time for CB > BM > PBSC)




10-14 days




Graft-versus-host




disease (GVHD)




Yes, skin, liver, GI most commonly affected




Acute (within 100 days)




Chronic (>100d, morbidity/mortality mo/yrs later)




No, but rare “GVHD-like” syndrome occurs in ~0.5% of auto-transplants (BMT2020;55:1879)




Graft-versus-tumor




(GVT)




Yes, major therapeutic goal is for donor T cells to engraft and attack host tumor cells




Likely no, but mechanism via CD8+ T cells under investigation (JCI2019;129:48)




Pharmacologic




Immunosuppression




Yes (usually 3-6 months; sometimes for 1-2y if GVHD develops)




No





ALLOGENEIC HEMATOPOIETIC CELL TRANSPLANT (NEJM 2006;354:1813)





• Donor types: matched to pt by HLA typing to minimize GVHD; matching at alleles A, B, C, DR, DQ




◦ Matched-related donor (MRD): compatible siblings, matched at 10/10 HLA alleles




◦ Matched-unrelated donor (MUD): NMDP database, matched at 8-9/10 HLA alleles




◦ Haploidentical: any parent/sib/child (~universal), match at 5/10 HLA alleles, ↑GVT via NK cells (FrontImmun2020;11:191)







Cell Source




Collection




Engraft




GVHD Risk




Notes




Bone marrow (BM)




Aspirated from iliac crest




18-21d




(Reference)




Less often used despite lower cGVHD risk, due to slower/less effective engraftment




Peripheral blood




(PBSC)




Mobilization and peripheral apheresis




12-15d




Higher risk




Generally preferred source due to faster engraftment (CochraneRev2014)




Cord blood (CB)




(Blood2013;122:491)




Immature cells from umbilical cord at delivery




28d (variable)




Lower risk




↑txp-mortality compared to MUD; allows for more HLA disparity





• Conditioning regimens (Blood2014;124:344): determined by underlying condition, disease status, and performance status




◦ Myeloablative conditioning: complete disease eradication & ablation of host BM/immune cells




▪ Used for young healthy patients, in remission or with measurable residual disease (MRD) (JCO2020;38:1273) ↑toxicity, ↑immunosuppression, ↑txp-mortality, ↓relapse




◦ Reduced intensity conditioning (RIC): tumor debulking & allows for engraftment




▪ Permits transplant in elderly w/ co-morbidities; ↓toxicity, ↓txp-mortality, ↑relapse (JCO2017;35:1154)




◦ Conditioning agents: chemo (e.g.,fludarabine, busulfan, cyclophosphamide, melphalan) ± total body irradiation




TERMINOLOGY
• One-liners include: underlying diagnosis; autologous vs allogeneic transplant; day since transplant (transplant = d0, day before = d-1, day after = d+1); conditioning regimen (myeloablative vs RIC/non-myeloablative); donor type (MRD, MUD, haploidentical), cell source (BM, PBSC, CB), GVHD prophylaxis regimen (e.g. tacro vs. cyclosporine, methotrexate, etc.)




• Example one-liner: 35M w/ AML (FLT3-mutated) who is now day +4 from his myeloablative (Bu/Cy) matched related donor (MRD) peripheral blood hematopoietic-cell transplant (PBHCT) with tacrolimus/methotrexate GVHD prophylaxis (day 0 = 1/1/21).




INFECTIOUS COMPLICATIONS: 2/2 chemo-related pancytopenia & immunosuppression (ASBMT/IDSA: BBMT 2009;15:1143)




Day 0-30




Pre-Engraftment




Day 30-100




Early Post-Engraftment




Day 100+




Late Post-Engraftment




Immune Defect




Neutropenic, mucositis, lines, acute GVHD




Poor cellular immunity, acute GVHD




Poor cellular and humoral immunity, chronic GVHD




Bacterial




GPCs & GNRs (F&N) Neutropenic enterocolitis (typhlitis)




GPCs & GNRs




Encapsulated bacteria (SHiN)




Nocardia




Viral




Resp/enteral (adeno, flu, RSV, paraflu), HSV




Resp/enteral (adeno, flu, RSV, paraflu), EBV (risk of PTLD), CMV, HHV6 (screen for in CB tx)




Resp/enteral (adeno, flu, RSV, paraflu), EBV (PTLD), VZV, BK (hemorrhagic cystitis), JC (PML)




Fungal




Aspergillus, candida




Aspergillus, candida, PJP




Aspergillus, PJP




Parasitic




-




Toxo




Toxo (can mimic PJP PNA)





• Neutropenic enterocolitis (typhlitis): polymicrobial infxn leading to necrotizing enterocolitis, most often involving cecum




◦ S/Sx: fever, ANC <500, abdominal pain (often RLQ), n/v, watery/bloody diarrhea




◦ Micro: polymicrobial (GPC/GNR/anaerobes/fungal), clostridium septicum a/w fulminant course & high mortality rate




◦ Dx: CT (I+/O+) w/ bowel wall thickening, mesenteric stranding, bowel dilatation, mucosal enhancement, pneumatosis




◦ Tx: pip/tazo vs cefepime/MNZ + surgery c/s + add fungal coverage if persistently febrile >72h




• Infectious PPX: items with asterisks (*) have well-established benefit and are employed at all institutions




◦ Bacterial: cipro 500mg BID or levofloxacin 500mg qd (day -1 to ANC >500)




◦ Viral (HSV/VZV)*: acyclovir 400mg BID or famciclovir 500mg BID (day -1 to +365 [auto]; 1y minimum & until off IS [allo])




◦ CMV: letermovir 480mg qd (dose-reduced w/ cyclosporine) used in CMV-seropositive recipients (day +7 to +100)




▪ Alternative: weekly CMV VL (day -1 to +100), with pre-emptive therapy for viremia with IV ganciclovir or PO valganciclovir




◦ Fungal*: fluconazole 400mg qd, vori 200mg BID, posaconazole 200mg TID (day -1 to ANC>500 [auto] or 3-6mo [allo])




▪ Anti-mold (vori-, posa-, isavu-conazole) prophlyaxis is considered in patients with AML, lengthy neutropenia




◦ PCP/Toxo*: Bactrim SS qd (start after engraftment as outpatient for 6mo [auto], >1y or off IS [allo])




• Acute GVHD: D0 to +100. ~40% in MRD, ~60% in MUD (cellular immune response, TH1 cell-mediated) (NEJM2017;377:2167)




◦ Risk factors: ↑HLA mismatch, ↑age, female donor/male recipient, donor parity, TBI-myeloablation, PBSC > BM > CB




◦ Cause: (1) Short-lived donor T cells react immediately; (2) Post-engraft, chronic infl → DAMPs/PAMPs → organ damage




◦ S/Sx: skin (rash, graded by biopsy findings, % body surface, desquamation), liver (cholestatic injury, graded by bilirubin), GI (diarrhea, graded by volume of diarrhea/day). Grading here.




◦ DDx: skin (viral, drug, engraftment), liver (viral, drug, SOS, TPN), GI (C. diff, CMV, adeno, GNR, typhlitis, drug)




◦ Tx: Grade I topical, II-IV IV methylpred 1-2mg/kg; if severe or steroid-refractory: vedolizumab, MMF, ruxolitinib (NEJM 2020;382:1800), antithymocyte globulin (ATG). Trial enrollment for cell therapies (MSCs, Tregs) (Blood 2020;136:410)




• Chronic GVHD: 30-70% of patients s/p allo-HSCT (humoral immune response, TH2 cell-mediated) (NEJM2017;377:2565)




◦ Cause: Pro-inflammatory environment iso graft-vs-tumor response, infx → iatrogenic thymic dysfx in training new T cells + Treg depletion → chronic inflammation w/ T/B cells → aberrant tissue repair after multiple injurious cycles → fibrosis




◦ Risk factors: prior acute GVHD, HLA mismatch, ↑age, PBSC > BM




◦ S/Sx: resembles scleroderma (sicca, dysphagia, arthritis, skin tightening, malar rash), lung (bronchiolitis obliterans), liver (cholestasis), cytopenias/immunodeficiency; any organ system (see NIH consensus scoring sheet in BBMT2015;21:389)




◦ Tx: steroid ± broad immunosuppression, photopheresis for skin; novel therapies including ruxolitinib, ibrutinib & belumosudil (ROCK2 inhibitor) have shown responses in steroid-resistant disease; cell therapies (BBMT 2020;26:835)




• GVHD PPX: day -3 to indefinite (tapered over months to years), goal to prevent graft rejection & acute/chronic GVHD




◦ T cell depletion regimens: (ATG, decreased T-cell dose) no longer favored; ↓chronic GVHD but no effect on survival




◦ Post-transplant cyclophosphamide: combined with tacro/MMF, previously used most widely for haplo and MMUD, now considered standard of care for all donor types ↓a/cGVHD, ↑infections







Immunosuppressant




Mechanism




Dosing




Toxicities




Tacrolimus




Calcineurin inhibitor




Trough goal: 5-10ug/L




AKI, ↑K, ↓Mg, ↑LFTs, n/v, TMA, tremor, DM risk




Sirolimus




(Rapamycin)




mTOR inhibitor




Trough goal: 3-12ug/L




AKI, sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS), leukopenia, TMA, HLD, cytopenias




Methotrexate




(MTX)




Anti-metabolite (inhibits thymidine)




Given on day +1,3,6,11 w/ tacrolimus




Mucositis, myelosuppression, hepatitis, AKI




Mycophenolate




(MMF/Cellcept)




Anti-metabolite (inhibits purines)




N/A




Myelosuppression, n/v/d




Post-transplant




cyclophosphamide




(PTCy)




Expands Treg, limits allo-reactivity (JCI 2019;129:2357)




Given days +3 and +4, particularly for haploidentical




Hemorrhagic cystitis, mucositis, cardiac toxicity





NON-INFECTIOUS COMPLICATIONS: immune-mediated organ damage, toxic effects of chemo, or immunosuppression



Q U I C K R E F E RE N CE : MG H E L L U C I D (day -8 conditioning to day +30 engraftment)




Monitor S/Sx




DDx fever




DDx abdominal pain




DDx dyspnea/hypoxemia




• Chemo toxicity: mucositis, N/V/D, S/Sx of infection




• GVHD: rash, jaundice, diarrhea (24h volume)




• SOS: RUQ pain, jaundice, ascites, edema




• Engraftment




syndrome: fever, dyspnea, edema




• Infection (bacterial, viral, fungal, parasitic)




• Drug reaction




• Engraftment syndrome (day 7-9 for auto, day 14- 21 for allo)




• Tumor (initial lysis & cytokine release)




• Immobility (aspiration, DVT/PE)




• GVHD




• Neutropenic enterocolitis




• Colitis: C. difficile, CMV




• SOS




• GVHD




• Obstruction, ileus, constipation




• Existing disease: CHF, COPD, asthma




• PNA: bacterial, fungal, aspiration




• Volume (often on mIVF, transfusions)




• Drug: chemo-induced lung injury or cardiotoxicity




• Engraftment (pulmonary edema from capillary leak)




• Pneumonitis




• Alveolar hemorrhage




• PE, TRALI, GVHD





• Pre-Engraftment (day 0-30): common to have mucositis, nausea/vomiting, alopecia, rash, diarrhea




◦ Mucositis: most HSCT patients get some degree of mucositis; duration & severity are worse in allogeneic HSCT. Treatment is focused on pain & caloric intake. WHO grade: (1) erythema (2) ulcer, solid+liquid PO (3) liquid PO (4) NPO




▪ Pain: topical/IV opiates; low threshold for PCA




▪ Nutrition: TPN initiated if PO intake impaired by mucositis & expected to continue for ≥1w




▪ Palifermin (recombinant keratinocyte growth factor): might reduce duration & severity with select ablative regimens




◦ Engraftment syndrome: sudden PMN recovery causing cytokine storm and vascular leak




▪ S/Sx: fever, rash, weight gain, bone pain; if severe – pulmonary edema, ↑LFTs, AKI, seizures




▪ Dx: diagnosis of exclusion (DDx: infection, drug reaction, acute GVHD)




▪ Tx: high-dose IV steroids (discuss with attending prior to initiation of steroids)




◦ Pulm – idiopathic interstitial pneumonitis/diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH):




▪ Cause: direct cytotoxic injury to alveoli




▪ S/Sx: fever, hypoxemia, diffuse lung infiltrates (ARDS)




▪ Dx: bronchoscopy w/ serial lavage (r/o infection, blood) – progressively bloodier on serial lavage c/w DAH




▪ Tx: high-dose steroids; + for DAH: FFP for INR<1.5, maintain plt >50k; limited data for recombinant FVIIa




◦ Liver – sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS) (previously called veno-occlusive disease [VOD]):




▪ Cause: direct cytotoxic injury to hepatic venules leading to hypercoagulable state and microthrombi




▪ S/Sx: RUQ pain, jaundice, ascites/edema; ↑ALT/AST/TBili, ↑INR/Cr (if acute liver failure or HRS)




▪ Dx: Doppler US c/w reversal of portal vein flow, liver bx; Dx criteria: Tbili >2mg/dL (<21d post-HCT), hepatomegaly/RUQ pain, sudden weight gain (fluid) >2-5% baseline body weight (see criteria and grading: Br J Haematol 2021;190;822)




▪ PPX: ursodiol 300mg TID (admit to day +30); Tx: defibrotide




◦ Renal – AKI (DDx: ATN, hepatic SOS, aGVHD, thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA), TLS, ABO-mismatched transplant)




▪ Nephrotoxins: calcineurin inhibitors, acyclovir, amphotericin, aminoglycosides




▪ TMA: subacute onset ~ day 20, caused by endothelial damage 2/2 calcineurin inhibitors, conditioning, & GVHD




▪ TLS: considered in pts with significant disease burden at time of transplant; PPX: allopurinol 300mg qd




◦ Heme – graft failure, cytopenias, bleeding:




▪ Primary graft failure: persistent neutropenia without engraftment




▪ Secondary graft failure: delayed pancytopenia after initial engraftment (immune or infectious)




▪ Rx: graft failure may require re-transplantation (CD34 boost); transfusions with irradiated & leukoreduced products




DISEASE RELAPSE: #1 cause of death post-HCT. Mechanisms: immune escape, resistant clones that survive conditioning
• Treatment: post-transplant maintenance (e.g., gilteritinib in FLT3-ITD AML) (Blood 2023;141:1), donor lymphocyte infusion (DLI), salvage chemo, then second allo-HCT, clinical trials for novel therapies




• Hospice and/or palliative approach is appropriate in select cases

topics.title: CAR T cell Therapy

runs.t: SELECTED FDA-APPROVED CAR T CELL THERAPIES

topics.text:
MECHANISM OF ACTION (NEJM 2018;379:64)


• Chimeric antigen receptor T cells autologous cell therapy whereby T cells are collected from patient, genetically modified with construct encoding a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) that directs T cells against a tumor antigen. CAR T cells are infused into patient, where they persist in vivo




• CAR: transmembrane engineered protein consisting of extracellular immunoglobulin (antibody)- derived domains (ScFv), which binds a tumor antigen (e.g. CD19). The ScFv is fused to signaling (CD3z) and costimulatory domains (CD28 or 4-1BB) that cause T cell activation and proliferation




S E L E CT E D FDA-A P P RO V E D CAR T CE L L T HE RAP I E S




• Yescarta (axicabtagene ciloleucel - “axi-cel”; anti-CD19, CD28 co-stim domain)











• Kymriah (tisagenlecleucel - “tisa-cel”; anti-CD19, 4-1BB co-stim domain)




• Tecartus (brexucabtagene autoleucel - “brexu-cel”; anti-CD19, CD28 co-stim domain)




• Breyanzi (lisocabtagene maraleucel – “liso-cel”; anti-CD19, 4-1BB co-stim domain, 1:1 ratio of CD8+:CD4+ CAR T cells)




• Abecma (idecabtagene vicleucel - “ide-cel”; anti-BCMA, 4-1BB co-stim domain)




• Carvykti (ciltacabtagene autoleucel - “cilte-cel”; anti-BCMA, 4-1BB co-stim domain, 2 anti-BCMA camelid nanobody domains)




TOXICITIES (JNCCN 2024; BBMT 2019;25:625)


• In general, the anticipated management approach of disease specific treatment-related adverse events should be discussed with the attending of record as case-specific considerations are common




• Cytokine-release syndrome (CRS)




◦ At least Grade 1 occurs in majority of patients, <10% Grade 3. Typically 1-3d (up to 10-15d) post-infusion, lasts ~7d. Caused by cytokine release (IL‐2, sIL2R, IFNγ, IL‐6, GM‐CSF) triggered by CAR T cell engagement of antigen and in vivo expansion. ↑risk: bulky disease, baseline ↓platelets, ↑CRP. Axi-cel > Tisa-cel




◦ Signs/Sx: fever, ↓BP, ↑HR, ↓SpO2, malaise, rigors, anorexia, myalgia. Can affect any organ (CV, lung, GI/liver, renal, CNS), arrhythmias, capillary leak syndrome, HLH




◦ Dx: monitor for 7d post infusion for FDA-approved therapies (inpt or possibly close outpt); VS, basic labs, ferritin, coags, CRP, TLS labs. When suspicious, make sure to rule-out infection




◦ Tx: See table. Tocilizumab (anti-IL6R) 8mg/kg over 1h (≤800mg);







ASTCT CRS Grade




General Treatment**




1




Fever (≥38C)




Tylenol, supportive. If >3d, consider tocilizumab




2




Fever & HoTN not requiring pressors or hypoxemia on NC




Tocilizumab q8h PRN up to x4, add steroids as below if still ↓BP after 1-2 doses, IV fluids




3




Fever + ↓BP requiring pressor or ↓SpO2 requiring




HFNC, NRB




Tocilizumab as above,




dexamethasone 10mg IV q6h (or equivalent)




4




Fever + ↓BP requiring multiple




pressors or ↓SpO2 requiring BIPAP, MV




Tocilizumab + dex as




above. If refractory, consider methylpred 1g/d IV x3d w/ taper







siltuximab (anti‐IL6) and/or anakinra (anti-IL1R); 2nd line: steroids. If plan to treat CRS with steroids or anti-IL6, **always




discuss with the treating attending of record (even if overnight)**






◦ Broad-spectrum antibiotics (cefepime) if fever + neutropenia




• Immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS)




◦ Etiology: unclear; cytokine diffusion into brain (IL-1, IL-6, IL-15 a/w neurotoxicity), BBB disruption, CAR T cell trafficking to CNS




◦ Timing: typical onset 4-10d post-infusion, duration variable (14- 17d). Can occur w/ or after CRS, but CRS is not req. for ICANS.







Immune Effector Cell-Associated Encephalopathy




(ICE) Assessment Tool




Max




score: 9




A&Ox3 [+ hosp] (4 pts), naming [clock, pen, button] (3 pts), follows commands (1 pt), writes sentence (1 pt), serial 10s from 100 (1 pt)







◦ S/Sx: aphasia, impaired fine motor skills, seizure, motor weakness, toxic encephalopathy (see ICE & ICANS grade), rare parkinsonism w/ BCMA CAR T cells (Nat Med 2021;27:2099)




◦ Dx: neuro c/s, ICE score, ICANS grade. If grade ≥3: MRI brain w/ w/o contrast, EEG, LP (r/o infection), fundoscopy




◦ Tx: See table. Seizure prophylaxis starting on day of infusion (levetiracetam 500-750 mg q12h for 30d). Generally, dexamethasone +/- anakinra, treat CRS if present, but **first discuss with the attending (even if overnight)**




◦ Prognosis: generally reversible, rare fatal cases







ASTCT ICANS Grade




General Treatment**




Grade 1




ICE = 7-9, awakens spontaneously




Supportive




Grade 2




ICE = 3-6, awakens to voice




Dex 10mg IV x1




Grade 3




ICE = 0-2, awakens to tactile stimulus, or focal edema on neuroimaging, or brief seizure




Dex 10mg IV q6h or methylpred 1mg/kg IV q12h




Grade 4




ICE = 0, unarousable, seizure >5min or w/o return to b/l, or deep focal motor deficit, or diffuse cerebral edema, or raised ICP




Methylprednisolone IV 1g/d x3d or equivalent w/ taper. Can add anakinra if no response





• Persistent Hematologic Toxicity




◦ Can cause grade ≥3 anemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, and B-cell aplasia that persists months-years




◦ Mechanism unclear, a/w with decreased baseline hematopoietic reserve and inflammation (Blood 2021;138: 2499)




• Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis Like Syndrome (IEC-HS): Rare, 1% develop (see Anemia) (TCT 2023 HLH guidelines)

topics.title: Solid Organ Malignancies
topics.text:
Source content



Organ




Risk factors/screening




Diagnostics




Treatment




Breast




▪ Infiltr. ductal (70- 80%)




▪ Invas. lobular (5- 10%)




▪ Mixed ductal/lobular (7%)




▪ Inflammatory Breast Cancer (1-5%)




▪ Mucinous (2%)




▪ Tubular (1.5%)




▪ Medullary (1%)




▪ Papillary (1%)




Risk factors: Age, genetics (BRCA1/2, CHEK2, ATM, PALB2), FHx, obesity after menopause, menopause >55, chest RT, 1st birth >30, nulliparity, HRT, menarche <13y, EtOH, benign breast disease, tobacco, DES exposure




Screening:




▪ USPTF: q2y mammo 40- 74




▪ NCCN: q1y mammo >40 or 10y before earliest FHx if >30 or 10y after RT if >30




▪Dx bilateral mammogram (Bi- RADS), US, FNA or core Bx (> excisional Bx), breast MRI if young or to assess extent (good Sn, but Sp 72%)




▪Path review




▪FH, ± germline genetic testing & counselling




Early stage (I, IIA, IIB through T2N1):




▪ Breast Conserving Surgery ± RT (NEJM 2023;388:585) vs. mastectomy ± RT, HR tx, HER2 tx, or chemo if high risk




Locally advanced (Stage IIB T3N0, IIA-IIIC):




▪ Surgery + RT w/ (neo)adj. chemo & HR/HER2 tx




(Neo)adjuvant therapy:




▪ ER/PR+, HER2-: tamoxifen or aromatase inhibitors (AI) (anastrozole, letrozole, exemestane); no AI if premenopausal; ± ovarian suppression if high risk.




Chemo: AC-T (doxo, cyclophos [CYC], paclitax.) or TC




▪ HER2+: TCH(P) (trastuzumab, carboplatin, docetaxel, ± pertuzumab) or ACTH(P) (doxorubicin, CYC, paclitaxel, trastuzumab ± pertuzumab) + ER/PR tx if HR+




▪ Triple Neg: if early stage adjuvant chemo + PARPi (BRCA1/2), stage II/III neoadj chemo +/- pembro (PDL1), w/ adjuvant capecitabine +/- pembro +/- chemo.




Metastatic/recurrent (Stage IV):




▪ ER+: as above ± fulvestrant (ER antagonist); ± CDK4/6 inhibitor or everolimus (mTOR inhibitor)




▪ HER2+: THP (1st line) or T-DM1 (trastuzumab-drug conjugate), trastuzumab+lapatinib




▪ BRCA mutation: olaparib or talazoparib




▪ Triple neg: systemic tx




Colorectal




▪ AdenoCa (98%)




▪ Neuroendocrine




▪ Lymphoma




Risk factors:




▪ FHx, genetic, IBD (UC>CD), obesity, tobacco, red/processed meat, EtOH, adenomat. polyps, age




Screening (45-75yo): colo (q10y), flex sig (q5- 10y), CT colo (q5y), FIT (q1y), Cologuard (q3y), FOBT (q1y) for 50-75yo




▪ Colonoscopy




▪ CT C/A/P, CEA




▪ MRI for liver mets




▪ Pelvic MRI or endorectal US for rectal CA




▪ Molecular testing: MSI/MMR status in all, K/N-RAS, BRAF, HER2, POLE, POLD1, RET amp.




Colon:




I-IIA: surgery + observation, or capecitabine or 5- FU/leucovorin (IIA)




IIB-IV: surg, RT, systemic tx: FOLFOX (oxaliplatin, leucovorin, 5-FU), CAPEOX (capecitabine, oxaliplatin), FOLFIRI (irinotecan, leucovorin, 5-FU), FOLFOXIRI (irinotecan, oxaliplatin, leucovorin, fluorouracil), ± bevacizumab; nivo ± ipi or pembro




Rectal: low anterior (LAR) v abdominoperineal resection (APR) ± neo v adj chemoRT. Chemo as in colon cancer




Lung




▪ NSCLC (84%): adeno, large>SCC




▪ SCLC (13%)




Risk factors (NatRevCa 2007;10:778):




▪ Age, male, tobacco, asbestos, occup. exposures, lung fibrosis or COPD, exposure to infectious agents (TB, fungal), FH




Screening:




▪ USPSTF: Annual low dose CT chest for 50-80 yo current smokers with ≥20 pack-year hx OR quit within last 15 yrs (Annals2014;160:330)




▪ CT C/A/P, FDG-PET/CT, brain MRI




▪ PFTs




▪ Evaluate pathologic LNs with biopsy




▪ Molecular testing for NSCLC (EGFR, ALK, ROS1, NTRK1/2/3, MET exon14 skipping, RET, PD-L1) before systemic tx




NSCLC: IA: surgery ± RT; IB-IIIA: surgery if able ± adjuv chemoRT ± osimertinib or atezolizumab. IIB/IIIA unresectable, IIIB: definitive chemoRT + adjuvant




durvalumab IV: systemic tx as below:




▪ ChemoRT: cisplatin + docetaxel/etoposide/ pemetrexed; carboplatin + pemetrexed/paclitaxel/ gemcitabine/docetaxel




▪ Targeted inhibitors: EGFR (osimertinib 1st line, erlotinib); ALK/ROS1 (alectinib, brigatinib, lorlatinib); BRAF/MEK (dabrafenib/trametinib); TRK (larotrectinib, entrectinib)




▪ Immunotherapy (PD-L1+) pembro ± chemo. ipi/nivo, atezolizumab+ platinum+ taxane + bevacizumab




SCLC:




▪ Limited: surgery + chemo ± mediastinal RT




▪ Extensive (NEJM2018;379;2220): chemo & atezolizumab v durvalumab (maintenance immunotherapy) ± RT for lobar obstruction, SVC syndrome, bone/brain mets




▪ Chemo: platinum agents, etoposide, irinotecan




Organ




Risk factors/screening




Diagnostics




Treatment




Melanoma




▪ Superficial spreading (75%)




▪ Nodular (15- 30%)




▪ Lentigo maligna (10-15%)




▪ Acral lentiginous (<5%)




▪ Amelanotic (2- 10%)




▪ Ocular (5%)




▪ Mucosal (~1%)




Risk factors:




▪ Sun exposure (UVB > UVA), atypical nevi, high nevi count, FHx or personal hx, immunosupp.




▪ Familial melanoma with germline CDKN2A, CKD4, POT1 mutations




Most common somatic mutations:




▪ BRAF (V600E, V600K) 50%, NRAS 15-20%, KIT 10-15% (acral). Genetic testing for stage II-IV disease




▪ Biopsy of primary tumor (Breslow depth prognostic), LN sampling, CT C/A/P, brain MRI, & serum LDH for active surveillance and treatment response




▪ Liver MRI for ocular/uveal melanoma




– liver most common




metastatic site




Localized disease: 0-I wide excision of primary tumor ± sentinel lymph node biopsy. Ib-II Topical wide excision +/- pembro/nivo (IIb/IIc) +/- RT, if surgery contraindicated or as adjuvant tx topical thx.




Metastatic disease: Systemic therapy ± excision (if feasible) ± RT (for sympt. localized disease, e.g. brain mets) ± talimogene laherparepvec (T-VEC, intralesion injection of HSV " tumor cell lysis & GM-CSF expression)




Systemic therapy: Immunotherapy (NEJM2015;373:23; NEJM 2015;372:2521): anti-PD-1 (pembro/nivo); anti-CTLA4 (ipilimumab), ipi+nivo (NEJM2019;381:1535). Targeted tx (NEJM2014;371:1867): If BRAF/MEK mutated, combo inhibitors(dabrafenib+trametinib, vemurafenib+cobimetinib, encorafenib+binimetinib). If KIT mutant, imatinib.





Source content



Pancreas




▪ Exocr./adeno (~95%)




▪ Endocrine (<5%)




Risk factors:




▪ Tobacco, EtOH, obesity, DM, chronic pancreatitis, age, male, FHx, HNPCC, chemical/heavy metal exposure, germline mut. (BRCA1/2, TP53, STK11, MLH1, MSH2/6, PMS2, CDKN2A).




Genetic mutations:




▪ KRAS, TP53, SMAD4, TGFbR1/2, CDKN2A, MLL2/3, KDM6A, ATM, NTRK, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, HER2, PALB2




▪ CT C/A/P pancreas protocol, EUS+Bx, MRCP ± ERCP, MRI for indeterminate lesions, PET/CT in high risk patients




▪ CA19-9, LFTs




▪ Germline testing +molecular profiling of tumor tissue




▪ Bx metastatic site if metastatic disease




▪ Resectable/Borderline: surgery ± systemic tx: 1st line FOLFIRINOX (leucovorin, 5-FU, irinotecan, oxaliplatin), modified-FOLFIRI, gemcitabine+nab-paclitaxel, gem+capecitabine, ± chemoRT




▪ Locally advanced: systemic tx as above or stereotactic body radiation (SBRT)




▪ Metastatic: systemic tx ±:




• BRCA1/2: olaparib (NEJM2019;381:317);




• NTRK fusions: larotrectinib, entrectinib




• MSI-H/dMMR/TMB-H: pembrolizumab (NEJM 2015;372:2509)




• BRAF V600E: dabrafenib + trametinib




Prostate




▪ Adenocarcinoma (95%)




▪ Transitional, basal cell, intraductal carcinomas; neuroendocrine, carcinosarcoma, lymphoma, stromal sarcoma




Risk factors:




▪ Age, black race, genetic factors (BRCA1/2, PALPB2, CHEK2, P53, MSH/MLH, FANCA) and family history), smoking




Screening with PSA:




▪ 40-75 high risk, q1-2 yrs if PSA <3, normal DRE




▪ 55-69: avg risk individual risk- benefit discussion, PSA <1 (q2-4 yrs)




▪ 70 and above: no testing (JAMA2018;319:1901)




USPTF: 55-69, individual risk- benefit per above.




Diagnosis: Bx




After diagnosis:




▪ TRUS, MRI, biomarkers, CT C/A/P, bone scan




Germline testing:




▪ High/very high NCCN risk




▪ Any risk level if +FHx or intraductal histology




Very low risk: surveillance (PSA, DRE ± Bx) if > 10 yr expected survival, if < 10 yr no intervention.




Low risk: surveillance vs external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) ± brachytherapy (BT) vs radical prostatectomy, if < 10 yr survival observe.




Intermediate/high risk: combination of EBRT, BT ± prostatectomy w/ lymph node dissection, and androgen




deprivation therapy (ADT): Orchiectomy, Androgen R blocker: enzalut-, apalut-, darolut- , flutamide. Androgen synthesis inhib: abiraterone (very high risk). GnRH agonist: leuprolide, gose-, hist-, triptorelin,




GnRH antagonist: degarelix, relugolix.




Metastatic/recurrent: ADT, if fail, ADT+doxetaxel. Bone




mets: radium-223 or denosumab/zoledronic acid, palliative RT. MSI-H/dMMR/highTMB: pembro if fail ADT.




Cancer of Unknown Primary




▪ Adenocarcinoma or carcinoma not otherwise specified (85%)




▪ Squamous cell carcinoma (5%)




▪ Undifferentiated carcinoma (5%)




▪ Neuroendocrine tumors (5%)




Pathologic Diagnosis:




▪ Core needle biopsy (preferred) and/or FNA from accessible site




▪ MSI/MMR testing




Initial Evaluation:




▪ Immunohistochemistry




▪ Gene expression profiling




▪ Tumor serum markers: β-hCG (testicular), AFP (testicular, hepatocellular carcinoma), CEA (CRC), CA-125 (ovarian)




Workup:




▪ Complete H&P (breast, GU, pelvic, rectal, skin exams)




▪ Routine labs (CBC, electrolytes, LFT, Cr)




▪ Occult blood stool testing




▪ CT C/A/P with IV contrast +/- PET




▪ Endoscopy, UA, LDH (if indicated)




Adenocarcinoma: paclitaxel + carboplatin ± etoposide; gemcitabine + cisplatin or docetaxel; capecitabine + oxaliplatin (CapeOx); fluorouracil + leucovorin + oxaliplatin (FOLFOX) or irinotecan (FOLFIRI); docetaxel + carboplatin or cisplatin




Squamous cell carcinoma: Paclitaxel + carboplatin or cisplatin; gemcitabine + cisplatin; docetaxel + carboplatin or cisplatin; cisplatin + fluorouracil; docetaxel + cisplatin+ fluorouracil (DCF)




Adenocarcinoma and SCC: capecitabine, fluorouracil, pembrolizumab, selpercatinib




Neuroendocrine tumors: paclitaxel + carboplatin + etoposide; cisplatin + etoposide; temozolomide ± thalidomide.

topics.title: Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors

panels.title: IRAES: DEFINITION, DIAGNOSIS, GRADING, AND MANAGEMENT (ASCO: JCO 2021;39:4073; NCCN Guidelines 2024)

topics.text:
IMMUNE CHECKPOINT INHIBITORS (ICI)
• Mechanism of Action: Block receptors that suppress T cell activation → CTLA-4, PD-1, LAG-3 (on T-cell) or its ligand e.g. PD- L1 (on cancer cell) → ↑antitumor immune response (Cell2023;186:1652)




Indications: ~10 drugs approved for 15 cancers. Prior autoimmunity not absolute C.I., but can cause flares (Cancer202012:738)




IRAES: DEFINITION, DIAGNOSIS, GRADING, AND MANAGEMENT (ASCO: JCO 2021;39:4073; NCCN Guidelines 2024)
• Definition: Immune related adverse events (irAE) are systemic autoimmune/inflammatory events 2/2 ICIs, involving any organ system w/ variable timing. Some data show irAEs a/w improved survival, even if hospitalization (JAMA NetwOpen 2024)




• Most common irAE sites: skin, liver, colon, renal, CNS, peripheral neuro, endocrine (hypoT), MSK, heme, pulm




• Inpatient Mgmt: Consult SIC (Severe Immunotherapy Complications) service for inpatient questions regarding concern for IRAEs. .




Select IRAEs: COMPRHENSIVE GRADING AND MANAGEMENT GUIDELINES (JCO Oncology Practice 2022; 18:6).




1. Skin toxicity: Common, 30-40% of pts (CTLA-4 > PD-1/L1 blockade). Rash, pruritis, bullous derm, lichen planus, psoriasis, rarely




SJS/TEN/DRESS. Vitiligo seen in melanoma, rarely in other cancers, a/w response to immunotherapy (JNCCN 2024; 22:9).




• Timing: Early, within the first few weeks after tx initiation




• S/Sx: Four types (1) Inflammatory (2) Immunobullous (3) Keratinocyte alteration (4) Immune reaction mediated




• Dx: exam; r/o other etiologies (infection, DRESS, SJS/TEN); grading based on BSA (<10% Gr 1, 10-30% Gr 2, >30% Gr 3)




• Tx: topical steroids, oral antihistamines for inflammatory/pruritic reaction. If severe, consider systemic steroids + derm c/s




irAE Severity and Grading









Severity




General Approach




Grade 1




• Continue Checkpoint Inhibitor (if no CNS / heme /




cardiac irAE)




• Increased freq. of monitoring




Grade 2




• Delay Checkpoint Inhibitor




• PO steroids OP (0.5 – 0.1 mg/kg), taper 2-4 weeks




• Re-challenge w/ ICI if returns to Grade 1 or resolved




• Increased freq. of monitoring




Grade 3




• Delay Checkpoint Inhibitor




• PO steroids OP (1 – 2 mg/kg), taper 4-6 weeks, IV




if symptoms persist 48-72 hrs




• Consider organ specialist consult




Grade 4




• Discontinue checkpoint inhibitor (except




endocrinopathies managed w HR)




• Inpatient IV steroids w/ taper




• Consult organ specialist





2. Colitis: More common w/ anti-CTLA-4; grade 3/4




colitis is higher with ipilimumab (<10%) than with anti- PD-1 agents (1-2%). (JITC 2018; 6:95).




• Timing: 6-8w after initiation of therapy




• S/Sx: Diarrhea, weight loss, abdominal




pain/urgency/rectal bleeding if severe




• Dx: Lactoferrin/calprotectin; r/o other etiologies (C




diff., stool Cx, etc.). CT A/P can show mild diffuse bowel thickening or segmental colitis. EGD/flex sig/colo for Grade ≥2 sx, path w/ active acute colitis.




• Tx: Antidiarrheal agents, budesonide 9mg PO or




prednisone PO vs. high dose steroids w/ taper, infliximab in refractory cases.




3. Pneumonitis: More common w/ anti-PD-1, serious




toxicity rare. Higher risk w/ combination therapy.




• Timing: Highly variable, can be later in therapy.




(Immunother Cancer 2020; 8:e000840)




S/Sx: Dyspnea, cough, fever, acute interstitial






pneumonia/ARDS; 1/3 asymptomatic (JCO2017;35:709;ClinCancerRes2016;22:6051)




• Dx: Rule out other etiologies (e.g. PCP), workup w/ CT though often non-specific can show GGOs and/or nodular infiltrates. Consider BAL +/- biopsy if suspect Grade 2 or higher.




• Tx: Oxygen, glucocorticoids w/ taper (4-6 wks), diuresis, infliximab, mycophenolate mofetil or IVIg if severe or refractory.




4. Hypophysitis (JAMAOncol2018;4:173): Primarily w/ anti-CTLA-4 (3%), rarely w/ anti-PD-1/PD-L1 (0.5%). Mechanistically distinct




from other irAEs; possibly by direct binding of ipilimumab to CTLA-4 on normal cells of anterior pituitary (SciTranslMed2014;6:230).




• Timing: Median onset ~8w




• S/Sx: HA (common, can be severe), fatigue, n/v, dizziness, weight changes, hot flashes, cold intolerance, hyponatremia (anterior hypopituitarism), vision changes; usually without central diabetes insipidus (posterior pituitary spared)




• Dx: MRI brain/pituitary shows diffuse pituitary enlargement (generally resolves by 2mo); test hormonal axes: 8AM serum cortisol + ACTH and/or cort stim; TSH w/ FT4/total T4/T3; PRL; LH/FSH, serum testosterone/SHBG (in men); IGF-1




• Tx: Hormone substitution: Hypocortisolism: glucocorticoid replacement (prednisone 3-5mg daily) (Cancer2018;124:3706).




Central hypothyroidism: levothyroxine. Hypogonadism: consider testosterone replacement. GH deficiency: GH theoretically contraindicated due to active malignancy, although little clinical evidence




5. Myocarditis (JACC2018;71:1755): Rare but serious AE a/w high mortality (46% in severe myocarditis); risk higher w/combo tx




• Timing: Generally within 3mo (Oncologist2018;23:874; Lancet2018;391:933)




• S/Sx: Heart failure, arrhythmia (new afib, high grade AV block, ventricular tachycardia)




• Dx: CK, EKG, troponin, NT-proBNP, TTE, MRI and EMG ± endomyocardial Bx




• Tx: Discontinuation of ICI; high dose or pulse-dose steroids (1g IV, then PO pred 1mg/kg) (J Am Heart Assoc 2020;9:2); 2nd-line consider ATG/IVIg or infliximab/MMF/tacro (Oncologist2018;23:879). GDMT for HFrEF. Potential PPM need (pending prognosis)




Other irAEs (JCO 2019;36:1714): Inflammatory arthritis/myositis, PMR/GCA, nephritis, pancreatitis/DKA, adrenal insufficiency, hepatitis/cholestasis, myasthenia gravis, GBS, peripheral/autonomic neuropathy, aseptic meningitis, encephalitis/ADEM, optic neuritis, transverse myelitis, AIHA, ITP, TTP/HUS, aplastic anemia, acq. hemophilia, pericarditis, uveitis/iritis, episcleritis, blepharitis.

topics.title: Oncologic Emergencies

panels.title: METASTATIC EPIDURAL SPINAL CORD COMPRESSION (Seminars in Neurology 2010;30:245; Lancet Neurology 2008;7:459)
BRAIN METASTASES WITH INCREASED INTRACRANIAL PRESSURE (Ann Palliat Med 2015;4:225; JCO 2015;33:3475)
SUPERIOR VENA CAVA (SVC) SYNDROME (NEJM 2007;356:1862; CA Cancer J Clin 2022;72:570)

topics.text:
TUMOR LYSIS SYNDROME (TLS) (NEJM 2011;364:1844; JCO 2008;26:2767)
• Pathophys: 2/2 tx initiation or spontaneous in cancers w/ high turnover → release of intracellular metabolites (i.e. uric acid, K+, phos) → AKI (uric acid causes renal vasoconstriction, precipitates in tubules), seizure, CaPhos crystal deposition (↑phos → ↓Ca)




• Presentation: ↓UOP, weakness/cramps/tetany/perioral numbness, seizure, arrhythmia




• Risk factors: high risk (>5%): ALL/AML (WBC ≥100k), CLL (on venetoclax & bulky disease), Burkitts, stage 3/4 lymphoblastic NHL, bulky TCL/DLBCL; intermediate risk (1-5%): ALL (WBC <100k), AML (WBC 25-100k or <25k & ↑LDH), Burkitt, DLBCL, CLL (chemo-specific & ↑WBC), rare chemo-sens bulky solid tumor (e.g. germ cell tumors); low risk (<1%): HL, indolent NHL, CML, CLL (on alkylating tx & WBC <50k), MM, MDS, all other solid tumors.




◦ High risk substrate: WBC >50k, LDH >2x ULN, bulky disease (>10cm), old age, hypovolemia, uric acid >7.5, AKI/CKD, mediastinal mass, BM involvement, HSM. High risk agents: venetoclax (highest), CAR-T, daratumumab, rituximab, etc.




• Labs/workup: BMP (electrolytes, Cr, iCal), Mg, phos (calculate Ca-phos product), uric acid, LDH, CBC/diff, ECG




• Diagnosis (Cairo-Bishop criteria):




◦ Laboratory diagnosis: ≥2 criteria within 3d before or 7d after cytoxic therapy: uric acid ≥8mg/dL, K ≥6mEq/L, phos ≥4.5mg/dL, or Ca ≤7mg/dL. Criteria also satisfied if 25% change from baseline.




◦ Clinical diagnosis: laboratory dx & ≥1 clinical criteria: Cr 1.5x ULN, arrhythmia, or seizure




• Prophylaxis: Low risk → Oral fluids. Daily labs. Medium risk → Continuous IVF (NS) at 2-3L/m2/d. Allopurinol 2-3d before chemo until Day +1. BID labs. High risk → Medium risk measures + telemetry & q6-q8 Labs. Consider rasburicase




• Treatment:




◦ Hydration: D5-1/2NS or NS if hypoNa/hypovolemic @ 2-3L/m2/d. Maintain UOP ≥100cc/hr for excretion of uric acid and phos; diuretics PRN (prefer loops to ↓K) to maintain UOP and treat hypervolemia




◦ Treat abnl electrolytes: hyperK tx (e.g. lokelma), sevelamer, delay tx of hypoCa until phos normalizes or hypoCa is severe (tetany/arrhythmia) to avoid ↑CaPhos precip




◦ Allopurinol: 300-600mg/day (adjust dose if renal dysfunction). Can use febuxostat if hypersensitivity or advanced CKD.




▪ ↓ clearance of other meds (cyclophosphamide, MTX, 6-MP, azathioprine, ampicillin)




▪ HLA-B*5801 ↑prev. in East Asian, Southeast Asian, Black pts ↑risk of SJS/TEN, consider alternative tx




◦ Rasburicase (↑uric acid clearance; discuss w/ attending & ): 0.2mg/kg IV (but 3-6mg IV usually effective), administer if high risk, baseline renal failure, ↑baseline or rising uric acid >7.5/Cr despite allopurinol/saline, or volume overlaod




▪ Risk of anaphylaxis, methemoglobinemia. Contraindicated in G6PD deficient (can cause hemolysis); check G6PD early




◦ Renal replacement therapy: generally indicated if Ca-phos product ≥70mg2/dL2 (albumin-corrected Ca × phos)




◦ Other: Urinary alkalinization w/ NaHCO3. Contraindicated in hyperphos (↑CaPhos precip). .




HYPERVISCOSITY SYNDROME/LEUKOSTASIS (Blood 2018;132:1379)
• Etiology: (1) hyperproteinemia from monoclonal gammopathy (e.g. Waldenström’s macroglobulinemia) or polyclonal (e.g. cryoglob) (2) hyperleukocytosis/leukostasis seen in AML/ALL with blasts >50k (rare in CLL unless >400k WBC) (3) other: PV, sickle cell




• S/Sx: pulm (SOB, infiltrates) & CNS (blurry vision 2/2 retinal vein engorgement, HA, dizziness, ataxia, confusion, coma), fever, epistaxis → page Heme/Onc fellow & Clin Path resident for emergency viscosity study, notify attending to discuss pheresis




• Diagnosis: serum viscosity (↑Ostwald tube), SPEP, SFLC, WBC (often >100k, but can be lower if AML/ALL blast crisis)




◦ Lab artifacts from hyperleukocytosis: spurious ↑K (use blood gas K), falsely low arterial paO2 (use pulse oximeter)




• Treatment: always start with plasma volume expansion with IV NS




◦ Hyperproteinemia: plasmapheresis (aiming for resolution of symptoms); reduces viscosity by 20-30% per session




◦ Leukostasis: leukapheresis; cytoreduce (hydroxyurea); induction chemo; avoid RBC & plt transfusion (↑viscosity)




METASTATIC EPIDURAL SPINAL CORD COMPRESSION (Seminars in Neurology 2010;30:245; Lancet Neurology 2008;7:459)
• Primary CA: prostate, lung, breast > NHL, renal cell, multiple myeloma, Hodgkin’s




• Location: T (60%) > L (25%) > C (15%); multiple sites in 30%; ESCC score for spinal level (JNCCN2016;14:70)




• S/Sx: back pain (usually 1st sx; radicular, localized, worse at night/recumbent/valsalva) → gait instability/ataxia → sensory deficits (ascending numbness, saddle anesthesia in cauda equina), bowel/bladder dysfunction (urinary retention, incontinence)




• Exam: pain precedes other sx by ~8w, weakness/ataxia, paresthesia, ↑reflexes, ⊕ Babinski, ↓anal sphincter tone




• Diagnosis: STAT total spine MRI with cord compression/metastasis protocol, CT myelography if MRI not possible




• Treatment: after imaging, STAT page Spine Surgery AND Radiation Oncology




◦ Neuro deficits/pain: generally dexamethasone 10mg x1 IV, then 16mg PO daily (divided), taper once definitive tx




BRAIN METASTASES WITH INCREASED INTRACRANIAL PRESSURE (Ann Palliat Med 2015;4:225; JCO 2015;33:3475)
• Intracranial tumors present in ~10-30% of patients with metastatic disease; call Neurosurgery & Radiation Oncology




• Primary CA: lung > melanoma > RCC > breast > head and neck, thyroid, esophageal, non-esophageal metastatic GI




• S/Sx: HA (40-50%), focal neuro deficits (20-40%), cognitive dysfunction (30-35%), new onset seizures (10-20%), stroke (5-10%)




• Diagnosis: MRI w/ contrast > non-enhanced MRI or CT with contrast.




• Treatment: control vasogenic edema (dexamethasone 10mg IV x1, then 4-8mg IV/PO BID), consider AED (usually not for 1° ppx); avoid AC if concern for active hemorrhage; definitive treatment will ↓local recurrence: for multiple mets, stereotactic radiosurgery > whole-brain XRT (↑neurocognitive impairment can be mitigated w/ hippocampal avoidance/memantine) > surgery (JCO 2022;40:492)




SUPERIOR VENA CAVA (SVC) SYNDROME (NEJM 2007;356:1862; CA Cancer J Clin 2022;72:570)
• Etiology: external compression of SVC from mediastinal mass (commonly lung CA or NHL) causing ↑upper body venous pressure




• Sx: raised ICP, narrowing of larynx/pharynx (dyspnea, stridor), head/neck swelling (visually striking), hemodynamic instability




• Diagnosis: CT venography (SVC syndrome protocol), obtain/ensure tissue diagnosis ASAP to guide definitive tx




• Treatment: secure airway, RT/chemo, intravascular stent (emergent if refractory sx), steroids (resp distress only, d/w attending)

topics.title: Febrile Neutropenia
topics.text:
DEFINITIONS AND ETIOLOGY (J Oncol Pract 2019;15:19)
• Definition: T ≥100.4 (≥1hr or oral >100.9) with ANC <500 cells/mL or <1000 cells/mL with predicted decrease to <500 over 48hr




• Microbiology: ONLY ~40-50% cases have infectious source identified; others attributed to translocation of intestinal bacteria




◦ When organisms identified: 40% GNRs (E. coli, Klebs > PsA); 60% GPCs (CoNS > MSSA/MRSA, strep, enterococcus/VRE) esp w/ indwelling lines or mucositis; fungal (Candida, molds) more likely w/ prolonged ↓ANC, broad-spectrum abx use, or TPN




EVALUATION
• H&P: comorbidities, type & time since last chemo, prior micro data, recent antibiotic therapy/ppx, medications, vascular devices




• Exam: mouth (mucositis), skin, perineum/rectal (visual inspection, avoid DRE), indwelling lines/port (erythema/tenderness)




• Studies: BCx x2+ sites (≥1 periph, 1 per CVC lumen), UA/UCx, CXR, SCx/GS, resp viral panel, CMV PCR (if HSCT)




◦ Fungal markers: LDH, β-D-glucan; galactomannan if high risk for Aspergillus (HSCT, GVHD, neutropenia >10-14d)




• Further symptom-directed studies to consider:




◦ GI symptoms: CT A/P (evaluate for neutropenic colitis/typhlitis); stool culture, O&P, C. diff if diarrhea




◦ Pulmonary symptoms: CT chest ± bronch/BAL (especially if prolonged F&N), SCx/GS, MRSA nasal swab, RVP, urine legionella, and consider testing for endemic mycoses if characteristic CT chest findings + exposure hx




◦ Headache/sinus pain: CT face/sinus




• Risk stratification:




◦ MASCC Risk Index (JCO2000;18:3038) and CISNE (JCO 2015;33:465) can measure risk of F&N-related complications




◦ High risk: anticipated ANC ≤100 for ≥7d, inpt status at time of fever, co-morbidities/infections (renal/hepatic impairment, PNA, central line infxn), allogeneic HCT, mucositis grade 3-4, alemtuzumab use or CAR-T within past 2mo → inpatient management




◦ Low risk (JCO2018;36:1443):short anticipated ANC ≤100 (<7d), no co-morbidities, good performance status (ECOG 0-1), strong home social support → treated with PO antibiotics after brief inpatient stay versus strictly outpatient




TREATMENT/PROPHYLAXIS
• : (Clin Infec Dis 2011;52:e56, J Oncol Pract 2018;14:250)




• Empiric abx: within 1h; higher mortality for each hr of delayed abx (AntimicrobAgentsChemother2014;58:3799)




◦ Gram-negatives (PsA dosing): Initial antimicrobrials SHOULD target gram-negative pathogens, including PsA




▪ Cefepime 2g q8h (or ceftazidime 2g q8h), pip/tazo 4.5g q6h, or meropenem 1g q8h




▪ PCN allergy: confirm allergy; use Penicillin Hypersensitivity Pathway and test-dose cefepime or meropenem; consider allergy consult. If true allergy, use aztreonam (avoid in ceftazidime allergy - both share the same side chain) + levofloxacin




▪ High-risk ESBL: meropenem 1g q8h (2g q8h if meningitis)




▪ Low risk: IV -> PO regimen (discuss w/ attending); cipro/levoflox + amox-clav vs clinda (if PCN allergy); avoid if prior FQ ppx




◦ Gram-positives: NOT a standard part of FN empiric regimen (ClinInfectDis2011;52:56)




▪ Select indications: HoTN/severe sepsis, GPC bacteremia, catheter-related infxn (rigors with infusion, erythema on exam), SSTI, radiographic PNA, severe mucositis + prior FQ ppx + GNR coverage with ceftaz




▪ First line: vanc; if there is concern for VRE then daptomycin (unless pulmonary process) or linezolid




◦ Anaerobes:




▪ Indications: intra-abd source, C. diff, oral ulcer/periodontal infxn, post-obstructive PNA, necrotizing ulceration




◦ Fungi:




▪ Indications: F&N >4-7d despite abx, ⊕ fungal biomarkers, ⊕ CT chest (circumscribed, air crescent, cavity), ⊕ BAL Cx




▪ Micafungin 100mg q24h or Amphotericin 5mg/kg q24h (admin after 500cc NS). Consult ID if high suspicion




• Modification/duration: Recommended duration of empiric therapy varies between guidelines (Ther Adv Infect Dis 2022;9)




◦ Resolution of fever:




▪ Documented infxn: narrow abx and tx for recommended course, then consider switch to FQ ppx until ANC >500




▪ Culture negative: continue empiric treatment until afebrile & ANC >500 vs narrow to FQ ppx if afebrile x4-5d




◦ Fever continues >4-7d:




▪ Clinically stable: do not broaden abx or add vanc, consider other causes (e.g. engraftment, differentiation, GVHD, TLS, drug fever, thrombophlebitis, hematoma, hepatosplenic candidiasis), discuss w/ ID




▪ Clinically worsening: broaden abx ± fungal coverage, consider CT chest ± bronch to evaluate for fungal infxn




◦ Catheter-associated infection: also see Bloodstream Infections & Endocarditis




▪ Coag-negative staph, non-VRE Enterococcus: generally can keep line if IV abx + abx lock x2w




▪ Staph aureus, PsA, fungi: must remove line. For gram negative, d/w ID/attending, consider line removal vs. lock therapy




▪ Complicated infxn (e.g. endocarditis, septic thrombosis, bacteremia/fungemia >72h post removal): remove line, abx x4-6w




• Prophylaxis:




◦ Anti-microbial ppx: refer to NCCN guidelines for more specific indications




▪ Antibacterial (FQs): high-risk pts (heme malignancy) and attending discretion for intermediate-risk pts




▪ Antifungal (azole vs echinocandin): select heme malignancies during neutropenia and early post-HCT




▪ PJP (TMP-SMX, atovaquone): if ≥20mg prednisone daily for ≥1mo, purine analog, CD4<200, or post-HCT/CAR-T




▪ HSV/VZV (acyclovir vs famciclovir): heme malignancy on therapy, post-CAR T, or post-HCT (1-2 years)




◦ G-CSF: ppx reduces incidence and duration of FN when risk >20% but does NOT decrease mortality(JCO 2015;33;3199); consider adding if critically ill, anticipated prolonged neutropenia, PTLD, or HIV. Caution if leukemia (d/w attending)




Jessica Nino de Rivera

topics.title: Inpatient Chemotherapy Regimens
topics.text:
Source content



Regimen*




Protocol




Supportive Care




Leukemia




7 + 3




7d of cytarabine and 3d of anthracycline




Induction for AML




Idarubicin 12 mg/m2 daily x3days or Daunorubicin 60-90 mg/m2 daily x3 days Cytarabine 100-200 mg/m2 continuously, days 1- 7




Premedication: TTE given cardiotoxicity risk




Emetic Risk: High




Neutropenia Risk: High




Growth Factor: Filgrastim or Pegfilgrastim




Decitabine




(5-aza-2'-




deoxycytidine,




Dacogen)




28-day or 42-day cycle until disease progression or toxicity




MDS/AML: 20 mg/m2 IV over 60 min daily on Days 1-5




AML with unfavorable cytogenetic and/or TP53




mutation: 20 mg/m2 IV over 60 min daily on Days 1-10




MDS: 15 mg/m2 over 90 min q8h on Days 1-3 OR 20 mg/m2 over 60 min daily on Days 1-5




Premedication: anti-diarrhea med PRN, IVF and/or electrolyte replacement




Emetic Risk: Minimal-to-low




Neutropenia Risk: Moderate




Growth Factor: Filgrastim or Pegfilgrastim




5-Azacytidine




(5-Aza, Vidaza,




Azadine, Onureg)




28-day cycle until disease progression or toxicity




AML: 300mg PO qday on D1-14




MDS: Cycle 1: 75mg/m2/day for D1-7; Subsequent Cycles: 75 mg/m2/day q4weeks (Dose may be increased to 100 mg/m2/day if no benefit after 2 cycles)




Premedication: For first 2 cycles, antiemetic 30 min prior to each dose then PRN after 2 cycles if no n/v; neuro-monitoring for CNS tox




Emetic Risk: Moderate, Cycle 1-2




Neutropenia Risk: Moderate




Growth Factor: Filgrastim or Pegfilgrastim, Epoetin alfa




HiDAC




(High-Dose ara-C)




(ara-C, Cytarabine)




Consolidation:




HiDAC: 1.5-3 g/m2 over 3h q12h on Day 1, 3, 5 -OR- Day 1, 2, 3 for 3-4 cycles 5 + 2: ara-C + anthracycline OR mitoxantrone 5 + 2 + 5: ara-C + anthracycline + etoposide




Premedication: Corticosteroid eye drops throughout consolidation




Emetic Risk: Moderate




Neutropenia Risk: Moderate




Growth Factor: Filgrastim or Pegfilgrastim




Hyper-CVAD




Dose-intensive phase: 8 cycles of Hyper- CVAD alternating with High-Dose Methotrexate and Cytarabine (HD MTX- ara-C) + intrathecal (IT) PPx each cycle for 16 IT treatments.




Maintenance phase: Dependent upon clinical response




Hyperfractionated Cyclophosphamide (CP): 300 mg/m2 IV over 3h q12h for 6 doses on days 1-3, given with Mesna 600 mg/m2 as continuous infusion ending 6h after last dose




Vincristine: 2 mg IV Days 4 and 11




Doxorubicin: 50 mg/m2 IV on Day 4




Dexamethasone: 40 mg daily on Days 1-4; 11-14




HD MTX-ara-C:




MTX: 200 mg/m2 IV over 2h followed by 800 mg/m2 IV over 24h on Day 1; Leucovorin rescue starting 24h after completion MTX; dose according to MTX level




ara-C: 3 g/m2 over 2h q12h x 4 on Days 2-3




Methylprednisolone: 50 mg IV twice daily Days 1-3




CNS PPx:




Risk-stratified CNS ppx with alternating intrathecal (IT) high- dose methotrexate (MTX) and cytarabine (Ara-C)




MTX: 12 mg IT on Day 2




ara-C: 100 mg IT on Day 8




Premedication: NS 100mL/hr prior to chemotherapy. Continue through cyclophosphamide




Emetic Risk: Day 1-5, high




Neutropenia Risk: High; Median times to granulocyte and platelet recovery were 18 and 21 days, respectively




Growth Factor: Filgrastim or Pegfilgrastim on Day 5 (24h after chemotherapy)




ATRA/ATO




Induction: ATRA should be continued until CR is achieved. Restage with BM aspirate and biopsy on Day 28




Induction:




All-Trans Retinoic Acid (ATRA): 45 mg/m2 in divided doses daily, starting Day 1. Start ATRA upon first suspicion of APL




Arsenic trioxide (ATO): 0.15 mg/kg IV daily, starting after cytogenetics confirmation




Consolidation:




ATRA: 45 mg/m2/d for 2 weeks q4wks for a total of 7 cycles




ATO: 0.15 mg/kg IV 5d/wk for 4 weeks q8wks for a total of 4 cycles




Premedication: None




Emetic Risk: Moderate




Neutropenia Risk: High




Differentiation Syndrome: maintain a high index of suspicion (fever; WBC >10k; SOB; hypoxemia; pleural or pericardial effusions). Discuss steroid use with attending, supportive




Growth Factor: Myeloid growth factors should not be used during induction. May be considered during consolidation for life- threatening infection




Hydroxyurea




(Hydrea; HU)




HU: Starting dose 500 mg BID or 1000 mg QD; dose adjusted to ANC 500-1000; cytoreduction and WBC count goal based on disease and therapy regimen




Premedication: None




Emetic Risk: Minimal-to-low




Neutropenia Risk: Moderate




Growth Factor: count recovery within days





Source content



Lymphoma




R-CHOP




14-day cycle, restage after 2-4 cycles, total 3-6 cycles +/- radiation




Rituximab: 375 mg/m2 IV Day 1




Cyclophosphamide: 750 mg/m2 IV over 30 min Day 1, combined oral and IV hydration 2-3L on day of chemo




Doxorubicin: 50 mg/m2 IV Day 1




Vincristine: 1.4 mg/m2 (max 2 mg) IV over 15-20 min Day 1




Prednisone: 100 mg PO Days 1-5




CNS PPx: 4-8 doses of IT MTX and/or cytarabine or high- dose MTX during the course of treatment




Premedication: Diphenhydramine and acetaminophen prior to rituximab, hydration for hemorrhagic cystitis risk




Emetic Risk: Day 1, high




Neutropenia Risk: High




Growth Factor: Filgrastim or Pegfilgrastim on Day 6 or 3-4 days after completion of chemotherapy until count recovery




Dose-Adjusted




R-EPOCH




21-day cycle, 6 cycles (dose adjustments based on ANC counts from BID CBC during previous cycle)




Rituximab: 375 mg/m2 IV Day 1




Etoposide: 50 mg/m2 infusion over 24h daily on Days 1-4




Doxorubicin: 10 mg/m2 continuous infusion over 24h daily on Days 1-4




Vincristine: 0.4 mg/m2 continuous infusion over 24h daily on Days 1-4




Cyclophosphamide: 750 mg/m2 IV over 30 min Day 5, combined oral and IV hydration 2-3L on day of chemo




Prednisone: 60 mg PO BID Days 1-5




CNS PPx: 4-8 doses of IT MTX and/or cytarabine or high- dose MTX during the course of treatment




Premedication: Diphenhydramine and acetaminophen prior to rituximab




Emetic Risk: Days 1-5, high




Neutropenia Risk: High




Growth Factor: Filgrastim or Pegfilgrastim after completion of chemotherapy until count recovery




R-ICE




14-day cycle, 3 cycles




Rituximab: 375 mg/m2 IV Day 1




Ifosfamide: 5,000 mg/m2 IV continuous infusion over 24h on Day 2 with NS at 1.5-3 ml/kg/hr beginning 2h prior and ending 2-4h after infusion




Mesna: 5,000 mg/m2 IV infusion over 24h on Day 2




Carboplatin: Dose AUC 5 mg/mL IV over 30 min on Day 2




Etoposide: 100 mg/m2 daily on Days 1-3




Premedication: Diphenhydramine and acetaminophen prior to rituximab




Emetic Risk: Day 1, 3 – Low; Day 2 High




Neutropenia Risk: High




Growth Factor: Filgrastim or Pegfilgrastim on Day 4 or 3-4 days after completion of chemotherapy until count recovery




ICE




See R-ICE above, hold rituximab





R-DHAOx




21-day cycle




Rituximab: 375 mg/m2 IV Day 1




Dexamethasone: 40 mg PO daily on Days 1-4




Cytarabine: 2,000 mg/m2 IV Day 2 (2 doses)




Oxaliplatin: 130 mg/m2 IV over 2h on Day 1




Premedication: Diphenhydramine and acetaminophen prior to rituximab




Emetic Risk: Moderate




Neutropenia Risk: High




Growth Factor: Filgrastim or Pegfilgrastim on Day 5 or 3-4 days after completion of chemotherapy until count recovery




R-Bendamustine




28-day cycle, 6 cycles




Rituximab: 375 mg/m2 IV Day 1




Bendamustine: 90 mg/m2 IV over 10 min or IV over 30 min daily on Days 1-2, CVC recommended for administration




Premedication: Diphenhydramine and acetaminophen prior to rituximab




Emetic Risk: Moderate, Day 1-2




Neutropenia Risk: High




High-dose




Methotrexate (MTX)




Dependent on chemotherapy regimen and count- recovery for 1-8 cycles




CNS Disease PPx and Tx:




IV MTX: doses of 500 mg/m2 or higher at varying times based on disease




Intrathecal MTX: 12-15 mg q2-7 days; continue for 1 dose beyond CSF cell count normalization




Leucovorin: 25 mg IV over 15 min or PO on Day 2 starting 24h from initiation of MTX and q6h until MTX < 0.05 uM




Hydration: Alkaline hydration with 5% Dextrose in sodium bicarbonate 100 mEq/L at 150 cc/hr 4h prior until 72h after MTX infusion




Emetic Risk: Days of MTX, moderate




Neutropenia Risk: High




Growth Factor: Filgrastim or Pegfilgrastim on Day 4 or 3-4 days after completion of chemotherapy until count recovery




Solid




FOLFOX, FOLFIRI,




FOLFOXIRI,




FOLFIRINOX




(FOL) Folinic Acid 1d (F) 5-Fluorouracil 1-2d (IRI) Irinotecan (OX) Oxaliplatin 1d




Folinic Acid: 200 mg/m² IV Day 1




Oxaliplatin: 85 mg/m² IV Day 1 Irinotecan 180mg/m² IV Day 1




Fluorouracil: 400 mg/m² IV bolus followed by 2400 mg/m² for 2 days




Toxicities: If acute cholinergic syndrome appears use atropine. Can also have laryngospasm and rarely, coronary artery vasospasm spasm (5-FU). Send DPYD gene test to screen for DPD deficiency.




Emetic Risk: High




Neutropenia Risk: High




Growth Factor: Filgrastim or Pegfilgrastim on Day 6 or 3-4 days after completion of chemotherapy until count recovery





*Chemo regimens may be modified based on genetics, risk stratification level, cardiac history, QTc prolongation. For further details on stratification and protocol details see NCCN.org

topics.text:
GENERAL APPROACH TO PAIN MANAGEMENT (WHO Guidelines; CDC guidelines; DFCI Pink Book
• A comprehensive pain hx is essential to guiding therapy. Goal is to maximize level of functioning and quality of life.




• Step-wise approach to pain management:




◦ Mild to moderate pain: non-opioids and adjuvants




▪ Acetaminophen: max dose 4g daily, 2-3g safe in liver disease (BrJClinPharmacol;2016;81:210)




▪ NSAIDs: celecoxib best if ↑GIB risk, ketorolac if severe pain [10 –15 mg recommended, no added analgesia with higher doses (AmFamPhys2017;96:262), use with caution in recent GIB, CAD, renal disease, IBD




◦ Moderate to severe pain: schedule non-opioid options, try topicals, then consider short-acting opioids PRN




◦ Severe pain: requiring round-the-clock opioids. Discuss w/ attending, consider adding extended release (ER) meds




▪ Avoid ER opioids if pain source is expected to resolve (e.g., bone fracture, hematoma, abscess, post-procedural)




• “Basal-bolus” strategy: Obtain basal level of pain control throughout the day with scheduled oral doses + PRNs for breakthrough pain




PAIN ARCHETYPES AND USEFUL ADJUVANT ANALGESICS
• Somatic/musculoskeletal: easily localized, sharp, aching, gnawing




◦ Bony pain: high dose NSAIDs or steroids*. Consider palliative XRT (if cancer-related) or surgery *Considerations with steroids: in




◦ Muscle spasm: topical lidocaine, capsaicin, methyl salicylate-menthol ointment; muscle relaxants cancer patients, may interfere with




(cyclobenzaprine, baclofen, tizanidine; watch for sedation & delirium) treatment (e.g immunotherapy)




• Visceral: deep tissues and internal organs, vague, referred or difficult to localize and/or diagnostics. If prolonged




◦ Visceral distension (e.g., hepatic capsular stretch from liver mets, malignant bowel obstruction): course, will need GI and PJP ppx;




depends on etiology but steroids* can be helpful. Can consider plexus block with Chronic Pain determine who will manage taper




• Inflammatory: associated with other signs of inflammation (swelling, erythema, warmth) plan at discharge




◦ NSAIDs (systemic or topical), steroids*




• Neuropathic: burning, stinging, allodynia, hyperalgesia




◦ Topical: capsaicin, camphor/menthol, lidocaine, diclofenac gel. POs in chart below (start low & go slow in older adults)




• Non-pharmacologic: PT/exercise/activity, heat or ice, CBT, treating comorbid psych dx, massage, acupuncture, other integrative therapies (note: for inpatient, massage and acupuncture currently only available for heme/onc patients including sickle cell)

KETAMINE (General Guidelines on Ketamine for Acute Pain, )
Initiation of ketamine, and adjustment of dose requires consultation with either Palliative Care or Chronic Pain Service




Consider in: 1) Expected severe post-operative pain (abdominal/thoracic surgery, orthopedic surgeries) 2) Opioid tolerant pts presenting for surgery or acute pain exacerbations. 3) Pts at increased risk of opioid-related respiratory depression (OSA)




◦ Adverse effects: rare at sub-anesthetic dosing (HTN, tachycardia, arrythmia, hallucinations, increased ICP, increased bronchial secretions,




N/V). Psychomimetic effects may be treated w/ 0.5-1 mg IV haloperidol or 1-2 mg IV lorazepam.




◦ Avoid in: poorly controlled cardiac disease, pregnancy, active psychosis/hospitalization hx (<3 yrs), severe liver dz, elevated ICP/IOP




OPIOIDS (CDC guidelines; 2022;11; DFCI Pain Management Pocket Resource; 2024;3)
• Below chart is for opioid naïve patients in moderate or severe pain.




• Opioid-tolerant defined as total daily dose (TDD) x7d: morphine 60mg/oxycodone 30mg/hydromorphone 8mg/ equianalgesic dose of another opioid. If opioid tolerant, consider home PO breakthrough dose or 10-20% of ER dose; if concern for hepatic or renal metabolism, would use wider dosing intervals and be more cautious with uptitration




• Patients on buprenorphine/methadone for OUD, or active non-Rx OUD → treat pain w/ full agonists if needed(See OUD & Withdrawal) . Can consult ACT if needed for assistance.




• Avoid using combo pills (limits titration flexibility). See Opioid Pharmacokinetics Chart below for sample initial dosing

◦ Cannot be converted linearly from other opioids

vasodilation → faster absorption)




◦ Requires 18-24h to reach therapeutic level





*Initiate with Chronic Pain/Palliative Care consult. Must ensure that there is an outpatient prescriber at discharge (PCP or subspecialist)

• If pain only moderately controlled with scheduled doses (not in pain crisis, no side effects), ↑ total daily dose by 30-50%.

• Rotate opioids if side effects, dose reduce by 25-50% when rotating (see box below and DFCI Pink Book, pg10)




• If pain persists, repeat pain hx, consider total pain, and involve an interdisciplinary team (eg, palliative care, chronic pain, etc)

PAIN CRISIS MANAGEMENT
Severe worsening of pain; while treating, pursue reasonable diagnostic workup for etiology (e.g., bowel perforation/peritonitis, procedural complication, bleeding). Goal is reduction in pain score by at least 50%. In sickle cell VOE, follow patient’s guidance/Acute Care Plan; if not showing improvement, engage SCD team early and adjust medication dosing as clinically indicated while awaiting their input.




1) Opioid-naïve: give morphine IV 2-5mg or hydromorphone IV 0.2-0.4mg bolus dose




Opioid-tolerant: convert usual breakthrough PO dose or 10-20% of total daily ER dose to IV and administer




2) Assess for response after 15min:




◦ No pain relief and no side effects → increase dose by 50-100%




◦ Minimal relief and no side effects (<50% reduction in pain score) → repeat the same dose




◦ Pain reduced >50% and no side effects → reassess in 2-3h, use this dose as new breakthrough dose




◦ Side effects with no pain relief → rotate to different IV opioid (no dose reduction if uncontrolled pain).




PATIENT-CONTROLLED ANALGESIA (PCA) (DFCI PAIN MANAGEMENT POCKET RESOURCE; 2024; 19)


• Appropriate for patients who are alert & oriented and able to use equipment. Families may NOT use PCA by proxy




• Requires daily delirium assessment (ie, CAM/4AT). Unrecognized delirium can obscure pain hx/medication use.




• Enables frequent administration of pain meds (vs max q1-2hr)

• Order “General PCA” (opioid-naïve pts) or “High Risk PCA” (BMI >40, hx OSA, RASS -2 to -5, age >65). If pt is opioid-tolerant, requires basal rate, consult Palliative Care/ Pain




• Increases in basal rate takes ~12 hrs to reach steady state: adjust basal rate q24hrs




ADVERSE EFFECTS OF OPIOIDS AND MANAGEMENT (DFCI PAIN MANAGEMENT POCKET RESOURCE; 2024; 20)
• Respiratory depression: Follows sedative effects. Hold opioid, consider low dose naloxone but CAUTION if on high dose ER opioids




◦ Dilute 0.4mg naloxone (1ml) in 9ml saline, give 1-2ml q2min until ↑RR or mental status improves. Naloxone half-life is 30-120min,




watch for recurrence of resp depression and consider naloxone gtt. All patients d/c’d on opioids need a naloxone script




• Constipation: ALWAYS start standing senna and/or MiraLAX when initiating opioids; use other laxatives if needed; methylnaltrexone QOD if failed laxative therapy (but can cause severe nausea/cramping; avoid if any concern for GI obstruction). (See Constipation, IBS, & Colonic Disorders)




• Opioid-induced hyperalgesia: generally seen w/ high doses (or lower doses in CKD), consider rotating opioids and involving pall care




• Myoclonus: reduce dose or rotate opioid, increase hydration; can give low dose BZD, or baclofen. If persists, c/s pall care




• Nausea/vomiting: tolerance to N/V may develop, start antiemetic on a fixed schedule for a few days. Suggest prochlorperazine, metoclopramide, haloperidol, avoid ondansetron (constipating). (See Nausea & Vomiting)




• Pruritus: mediated by mu receptor (not histamine – Benadryl ineffective unless rash/allergic reaction); consider opioid rotation, nalbuphine 5mg IV q6h prn, or low dose naloxone gtt




• Sedation: occurs prior to resp depression. Hold sedatives/anxiolytics/opioids, reduce dose, if persistent consider CNS stimulant (increased caffeine intake, dextroamphetamine or methylphenidate 2.5-5.0 mg PO daily, modafinil 100-200 mg PO daily), discuss w/ Pall Care team.




• Delirium: reduce dose or rotate opioid; IV Haldol 1-2.5mg BID-QID or IV/PO Zyprexa 2.5-5mg PO QD-BID

topics.text:
SERIOUS ILLNESS CONVERSATIONS MGH CONTINUUM PROJECT
When? Conversations can be planned or may happen spontaneously in any setting (NEJM2014;370:2506). Should discuss early in disease course as outpatient, or:




• New, progressive (eg, increasing hospitalizations/ED visits, intolerance of guideline-directed therapies), or life-altering serious medical illness such as advanced cancer, ESRD, ESLD, HF, COPD




● Prognosis trigger: “Would I be surprised if this patient died in the next year?” (JPalliatMed2010;13:837). Can use WalterIndex1year mortalitycalculator. Life expectancy <6mo ( JAMA 2001;285: 2987; JPalliatMed2012;15:175)




● Age >80 and hospitalized if no previous documentation (See Geriatric Assessment & Frailty)




Why? Longitudinal SICs help explore illness understanding, hopes/worries, and what matters most. Involves pt-centered recommendation regarding a care plan that aligns with pt goals. Can be used for the purposes of Advanced Care Planning, discussion of transition to hospice/CMO, or referral to palliative care (more than just code status) How?: Preparation for planned meetings:




• Consider consulting Palliative Care prior to the formal meeting if complex decisions/psychosocial issues/family conflict.




• Consider involving hospital ethics, the Optimum Care Committee (OCC), if you have concerns about the family’s preferences for patient care that do not align with the wishes of the patient or reality of the medical situation.




• Identify time and location to accommodate the patient and their loved ones, RN, SW, primary team, and consultants as applicable. Can be helpful to see if any long-term provider (PCP) is available to join.




• Prior to the patient and their loved ones joining, meet with the health care team to discuss: goals, unified assessment of




clinical scenario, if a clinical decision needs to be made urgently, and if so, what are treatment options and team




recommendations (in alignment w/ pt stated goals)




MGB Serious Illness Conversation (SIC Guide, Educational Videos): Thescript below can be adapted depending on whether you are talking directly to the patient vs the patient’s family.







Step




Suggested Prompts




Open the conversation




“I’d like to talk about what is ahead with your health. Would that be ok?”




Assess prognostic awareness




“What is your understanding of your health?” “Looking to the future, what are your hopes about your health? What else?” “What are your worries? Tell me more.”




Share worry




“Would it be ok if we talked more about what may lie ahead?” “I hear you’re hoping for ____ and I worry the decline we’ve seen will continue” or “I worry something serious may happen in the next few wk/mth/yrs.” “It can be difficult to predict what will happen with your health.”




Respond to emotion




NURSE mnemonic to respond to patient’s/loved one’s emotions (CA Cancer J Clin. 2005; 55:164):




Acronym




Name Understandin g Respect




Support Explore




Example




"It sounds like you are frustrated."




"I cannot imagine what it would be like to be in this situation."




"You’re asking all the right questions and doing an amazing job advocating for your husband."




"I will be around to answer any of your questions."




"Tell me more about what you are thinking."




Align




“I wish we didn’t have to worry about this.”




Explore what’s important




“What gives you strength as you think about the future of your health?” “If your health worsens, what is most important to you?” “How much do your family or friends know about your priorities and wishes?”




Make a recommendation




“It sounds like ____ is very important to you.” “Given what’s important to you, I would recommend______”





● Consider filling out ACP forms if not already filled out. See Advanced Care Planning Forms below




A DVANCE C ARE P LA NNING F ORMS
● Health Care Proxy (HCP)/medical power of attorney: an advance directive document that designates a healthcare agent to make future medical decisions if patient loses capacity. Expressly authorized in MA by statute. Filling out this form is a priority for all patients but more urgently for older adults, those with emerging cognitive impairment, and those with multimorbidity and/or complex life-limiting illnesses.




◦ If no HCP: see Section 3, bullet 6 of MA:AnActImprovingMedicalDecisionMaking




● Living Will: an advance directive document in which a competent person specifies future medical treatments in the event of incapacity (usually at end-of-life or if in a persistent vegetative state). Can be used as evidence of a person’s wishes, but not considered to have legal authority (no MA statute that expressly authorizes)




● MOLST (MA Medical Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment): medical orders for patients with multimorbidity or serious illness that documents preferences for CPR, intubation, hospital transfer, artificial nutrition, dialysis, and more




◦ Transferrable to outside facilities; must complete MOLST prior to discharge to rehab/SNF if patient DNR/DNI




◦ . Remember that you do not have to fill out or discuss everything on the back page




(clinical discretion). When filling out a new form, provide patients with a copy and scan into Epic for future documentation.




◦ Remember that these decisions can be changed (fill out a new MOLST if decisions change)




Source content
● Links to existing MOLST/HCP forms are found in Advance Care Planning Activity tab or scanned into the Media tab




CODE STATUS DISCUSSIONS
General Considerations




● Confirm directly with the patient/HCP, MOLST, and/or prior documentation by outpatient providers




● Readdress if a patient’s clinical status changes, or if code status appears discordant with the clinical setting, Do not need to routinely readdress on admission if has been recently addressed by outpatient providers




● Code status ≠ ACP. Code status is a medical procedure for which harms/benefits should be weighed iso clinical context.




● Many procedural teams (i.e. cards, surgery) require temporary reversal of DNR/DNI periop, often 30d (JAGS2022;70(12):3378-3389):




◦ If changing code status pre-op, ensure your discharge documentation includes changing status back/date of conditional




code status end




◦ If changing code status during early post-procedure or during chemotherapy, notify procedural team/primary oncologist




Survival Outcomes (Circulation2019;139:e56; JAMA 2019; 321:1200)




● Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: survival to hospital discharge 10.4%; survival with good neurologic function 9.9%




● In-hospital cardiac arrest: survival to discharge 25.6%; survival with good neurologic function 22%




◦ Favorable prognostic factors: ACS, drug overdose, drug reaction (up to 40% survival)




◦ Unfavorable factors: age >80 (<10% survival), multi-organ failure, sepsis, advanced cancer, ESRD, ESLD, dementia




◦ Post-arrest complications: hypoxic-ischemic brain injury, rib fractures, pulmonary contusion, prolonged ICU care, acceleration of




physical and cognitive frailty/disability




Code status options:







Full Code




The patient would want all resuscitative measures to be used




DNR/Ok to Intubate




The patient would not want cardiac resuscitation but would want to be intubated in the event of impending respiratory failure




DNR/DNI




In the event of a pulseless cardiac arrest or respiratory failure, the patient would not want cardiac resuscitation or intubation




DNR/DNI/LLST Comfort Measures Only (CMO)




The patient would want their care team to orient care around comfort only, and care not oriented around comfort may be withdrawn while still treating the patient’s symptoms




Do not offer “Full Code Except Do Not Intubate.” Cardiopulmonary arrest requiring CPR nearly always necessitates intubation, and thus this is not an appropriate code status.





Conducting Code Status Discussions (JAMA 2012;307:917)




• Suggested opener: “Have you ever discussed CPR and intubation with your medical team? I want to make sure that I understand whatever decisions you’ve made regarding those two interventions.”




• Suggested framing: “Resuscitation is a medical procedure we would perform if your heart were to stop and you died. What have you heard about resuscitation?”




• Many people would prefer a natural death. If you prefer a natural death, then we would protect you from these procedures and ensure your comfort.” Approaches to discussion of code status based on scenario (NEJM 2020;382:2450):







Scenario/Indication




Approach/Goal




Example




The patient has a stable condition and is likely to benefit from CPR/Intubation




Make sure the patient does not strongly prefer to avoid




“Right now, if your heart were to stop, you would receive CPR. Is this consistent with your goals?”




The patient already has a preference to limit CPR and intubation that needs confirmation




Confirm an already established preference




“Your records show that you made an emergency plan with your outpatient doctor to focus on comfort and allow for a natural death. This means that we would not use chest compressions to start your heart or a use a breathing machine. Based on my medical assessment, I think we should continue this plan now. Does that sound right to you? We will do everything else we can to help you get through this.”




The patient has an advancing illness, and it is unclear whether the benefits of CPR and intubation would outweigh the burdens (the decision depends heavily on the patient’s values and goals)




Shared decision- making




“If an emergency were to occur and your heart were to stop, it is difficult to predict what would happen if you received CPR or a breathing tube. Recognizing this uncertainty, if your heart were to stop and you were to stop breathing, what would you want your medical team to know about what is important to you?” “Given what’s important to you, I would recommend______”




The patient is at risk for decompensation/death, unlikely to benefit from CPR and intubation




Informed Consent




Introduce/assess: If urgent: “I wish we were meeting under different circumstances.”




Share information: “Given all that’s happened, I worry that your health has worsened. What are your thoughts about how things have been going?” (Discuss medical situation, share concerns using hopes/concerns)




Explore goals: “Given where we are, what is most important to you?” Make a




recommendation:




-“I recommend we make a plan to help you meet your goals and avoid treatments




that are unlikely to help.”
